CRASH TRAGEDY Husband and wife who died when light aircraft crashed are pictured after ‘challenging search operation’ in countryside

THE husband and wife killed in a horror plane crash last week have been pictured as tributes to the couple flood in.

Ketan Swali and Sheetal Swali were supposed to land at an airport in North Wales on August 14 but failed to appear.



Ketan, a member of a Staffordshire flying club, was remembered as being “popular”.

The club said in an online tribute: “Ketan was a very popular member and loved to talk about flying and aviation.



“Our heartfelt condolences go to their families and friends at this difficult time.”

Police were called to the scene at Caernarfon Airport at around midday before launching a multi-agency search for the light aircraft.

It was shortly afterwards found in a remote area near Trawsfynydd, Gwynedd where the two, both from Syston in Leicestershire, were pronounced dead.

A team of investigators from the Air Accidents Investigations Branch (AAIB) shortly after launched a probe into the tragedy.

Ch Supt Owain Llewellyn said: “Our thoughts are with the families and friends of those involved in this tragic incident.

“We will support the AAIB with their investigation to ensure the circumstances leading to this incident are fully understood.



“This has been a challenging search operation and I am grateful to all of the agencies involved for their professionalism and dedication.”

North Wales Police are supporting the AAIB in its probe into the tragedy.

TRAVEL CHAOS M25 grinds to a halt with 80-minute delays & SIX miles of traffic after two lorries crash

A MAJOR crash between two lorries has brought traffic on the M25 to a halt while emergency services clear the scene.

The two HGVs collided this morning on the clockwise carriageway between Junction 5 and Junction 6 at Godstone, Surrey.



Traffic officers and recovery teams are at the scene.

Two of the four lanes have been closed while emergency crews deal with the smash.



National Highways says drivers are facing delays of around 80 minutes.

They add that congestion is stretching for six miles on the approach.



Motorists are being warned to expect major disruption on the busy stretch of motorway.

News.title: Will there be a UK heatwave on the August 2026 bank holiday? Latest Met Office weather forecast
News.content:
WITH the August Bank Holiday a week away, Brits planning beer garden outings, coastal trips, or festival visits are keeping a close eye on the forecast.

Following mid-August’s blistering temperatures, the latest Met Office updates show that something of a meteorological shift is underway.



That could make a Bank Holiday heatwave unlikely, but the upcoming long weekend still looks set to offer some optimism for those with plans outdoors.

At the time of writing, the Met Office’s latest blog says that “after weeks of predominantly hot and dry weather,” the pattern across the UK has shifted.



That has brought with it “a very different feel“, with a “noticeable drop in temperatures.”

While early August brought scorching conditions, low pressure systems have broken the extreme heat, ushering in fresher, wetter conditions across many regions.



What is the forecast for the August Bank Holiday?

Looking ahead to the three-day weekend across August 29-31, the Met Office’s long-range forecast predicts a mixed bag.

The week will start on a promising note, with conditions “largely dry and settled” as “a ridge of high pressure continues to extend across the country.”

But forecasters say this calm spell will be brief as the long weekend approaches.

The Met Office says the weather is likely to turn “more unsettled during the week and through to the turn of the month as low pressure becomes more dominant.”



This change in pressure systems is set to bring “showers or longer spells of rain, perhaps heavy, to most if not all areas at times though still some sunny interludes.”

The forecaster adds that conditions could become “possibly windy at times too.”

Will there be a Bank Holiday heatwave?

In the UK, an “official” heatwave is declared when a location meets or exceeds a specific daily maximum temperature threshold for at least three consecutive days.

These thresholds vary by region to account for local climates, ranging from 25C in Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, and northern England up to 28C in London and the southeast.

If temperatures fall short of the local benchmark on any of those three days, the spell fails to qualify.



The Met Office’s long-range projection essentially rules out any prolonged extreme heat.

It forecasts that overall temperatures will remain “likely near to average though varying.”

But weather analysts say that there could still be “some short-lived warm and humid spells possible, especially in the south,” offering moments of summer warmth between unsettled weather fronts.

While the Met Office’s long-range computer models provide an idea of the weather ahead of time, the forecast will firm up significantly as meteorologists get within three to five days of the Bank Holiday weekend.

News.title: Classic novel given ‘Gen Z makeover’ to help parents understand their kids’ slang
News.content:
CHARLES Dickens’ classic novel ‘Great Expectations’ has been given a Gen Z makeover, reimagined in today’s trending youth slang.

Renamed ‘Bare Expectations’, the tale has been ‘translated’ into teen speak to help parents better understand the language their children use today, with the line “And what coarse hands he has! And what thick boots!” reimagined to read “She thought I was an absolute L, and my drip gave her the major ick.”



While “I was dreadfully frightened” now says “I was absolutely cooked”.

It comes after research of 2,000 parents with children between 10 and 16 found 70 per cent have struggled to understand a text message, social media post or online comment written by their child because of slang.



Commissioned by Tesco Mobile, this novel was recreated as ‘Bare Expectations’ to help families navigate the ever-changing world of teen language and is now available as an audiobook on Spotify and Apple Music .

It has been paired with a glossary explaining some of the most misunderstood words and phrases to help parents make sense of modern digital language and encourage conversations about online safety.

The modern-day adaptation has been launched alongside the mobile network’s new Safe Start offering – a guided phone-readiness experience, designed to help parents feel more confident that their child’s phone is safely set up and ready for day one.

The phone network partnered with Chloe Combi, author, researcher, and one of the world’s foremost experts on Generation Z and Generation A, to advise on the translation of the novel into modern teen slang and provide crucial insights into youth culture.

Chloe Combi said: ”Teen slang is evolving at an unprecedented pace. A word can emerge as a social media craze one day and become everyday language the next.

“’Bare Expectations’ funnily shows how much communication has evolved by translating a familiar story into today’s youth language, helping parents understand their children’s world and start more confident conversations.”



To bring the adaptation to life, Tesco Mobile partnered with Kurupt FM’s MC Grindah, who was invited to a youth centre in London to give a reading of ‘Bare Expectations’ to local parents and teens, highlighting the rapid evolution of digital language.

MC Grindah, who hopes the project helps families bridge generational language gaps, said, “You’d think the best MC in the galaxy would know all the latest slang, and I do.

“If any kid tells you otherwise, they’re lying. Any words I don’t know are just not cool enough for me to care about.”

The study also found 41 per cent of parents whose children use slang look up a word, abbreviation or emoji at least once a week in an effort to keep up with the latest terminology.

Among the most confusing expressions are ‘gyatt’ meaning strong excitement, surprise or admiration (37 per cent); ‘finsta’, meaning a secret Instagram – usually hidden from parents (37 per cent); and ‘mewing’ meaning holding your tongue against the roof of your mouth to try to define your jawline (34 per cent).



Parents were also stumped by ‘you’re clapped’ translating to ‘you’re ugly’ and ‘mogging you’ which transcribes to looking better than someone else.

The glossary and audiobook form part of the launch of Safe Start, which offers customisable parental controls, AI-powered social media monitoring through Sway.ly, and expert online safety resources to help families navigate the digital world with confidence.

Laura Joseph, the mobile network’s chief customer officer, said: “Parents don’t need to speak their children’s language to help keep them safe online, but they do need the confidence to start the conversation.

“With many parents telling us that teen slang and rapidly changing online trends can make it harder to spot potential issues, Safe Start is designed to help bridge that gap.

“By combining expert online safety guidance with AI-powered social media monitoring through Sway.ly, we’re giving families practical tools to better understand the digital world young people are navigating every day and support safer online experiences.”



Nearly half (49 per cent) of parents worry about inappropriate content being shared with their child, while 48 per cent fear strangers making contact online, and 40 per cent worry about bullying and exclusion.

And while parents said the hardest conversation they have with their kids relates to inappropriate content (27 per cent), 84 per cent chat to their child about staying safe online at least once a month, according to the survey by OnePoll.

Daniela Fernandez, co-founder of Sway.ly and who notes that parents want to protect their children online but often struggle to understand their digital world and language, said: “That’s why we’ve partnered on this new Safe Start SIM.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Our technology gives parents insights into their children’s social media use, alongside practical tools and guidance, so they can spot problems early and act with confidence.

“The ‘Bare Expectations’ campaign further helps families start important conversations for a healthier online experience.”

News.title: Eight unanswered questions surrounding Harry and Meghan’s UK comeback as couple plots return six years after Megxit
News.content:
PRINCE Harry and Meghan are coming back to Britain in a bombshell Megxit homecoming that could reopen old royal wounds.

The Sussexes are returning six years after quitting royal life and fleeing to America, raising questions over security, family feuds and their future role.



The Sun’s World Exclusive revealed the couple are set to return at the end of this month for an “extended period” with their children Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.

They have found a new UK home and are expected to remain in Britain while the youngsters are at school.



But the dramatic move leaves a string of awkward questions hanging over the Royal Family.

Security row: Who is funding it?

Harry has spent years fighting for taxpayer-funded security whenever he and his family are in Britain.



He launched a multi-million-pound legal battle to get his 24-hour armed protection reinstated, insisting it was unsafe to bring his family home.

Harry was seeking to overturn a decision that downgraded his security after the “Megxit” saga when he stopped being a working royal and moved to the US with his wife.



His lawyers had argued that he had been “singled out” for “inferior treatment”, but a senior judge ruled that Prince Harry’s “sense of grievance” did not amount to a basis for a successful appeal.

After suffering a “devastating” court defeat 18 months ago, he said: “I can’t see a world in which I would bring my wife and children back to the UK at this point.”

Though last month, Harry was back in the UK for the Invictus Games.

Harry flew to the UK alone and hours before arriving in London an invitation to stay at Buckingham Palace was reportedly withdrawn after he failed to meet the deadline for a decision.

Meghan, 44, meanwhile, delayed her arrival and entered the country in secret with the children.



While in the UK the Sussexes took their children to meet the King, with the meeting dubbed a “private family occasion” that took place out of the public eye.

It was their first family gathering since the shock claims made by the Sussexes in their six-part Netflix documentary, six months later.

It is believed during their stay they visited Diana’s burial site on an island in the middle of the Oval lake, on the Spencer family’s ancestral estate.

It is understood they will not receive money from the public purse while back in Britain, and Harry will not undertake official royal duties.

But it remains unclear whether there have been any changes to the Home Office’s security position, or whether taxpayers could ultimately bear any of the cost.



Tensions with the Royal Family: Will this better or worsen them?

Harry and Meghan’s homecoming comes after six years of public criticism of the Royal Family and Britain.

The couple quit as working royals in 2020 before moving to California, and have since given explosive interviews, released a Netflix series and published Harry’s memoir Spare.

Harry described royal life as “a mixture between The Truman Show and being in a zoo”.



He also said: “For most of my life I always felt worried, concerned, a little bit tense and uptight whenever I fly back into the UK.”

The couple made damaging claims about the Royal Family during their Oprah Winfrey interview, while Spare revealed deeply private family rows.

The King is believed to welcome the chance to see more of his grandchildren, and his meeting with Harry and Meghan at Highgrove last month appears to have opened the door to a closer relationship.

However, relations are clearly still strained between the Sussexes and the King since he was only made aware of their return on Sunday.

Despite the fact they must have been planning the move for weeks, if not months, the pair did not raise the prospect of a return when they met Charles and Camilla at Highgrove, Gloucs, in July.



Last year Prince Harry said the King “won’t speak to me because of this security stuff”, but that he did not want to fight any more and did “not know how much longer my father has”.

The prince spoke to BBC News in California after losing an appeal over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

The Duke of Sussex told the BBC he “would love a reconciliation” with the Royal Family in an emotional interview in which he said he was “devastated” at losing a legal challenge over his security in the UK.

Fab Four feud: Will William and Kate ever forgive?

The brothers were once at the heart of the so-called Fab Four alongside their wives, but the relationship has since spectacularly broken down.



Royal photographer Arthur Edwards believes the King may be prepared to give Harry another chance, but is far less convinced William will be ready to forgive.

Edwards wrote: “But while His Majesty may welcome back Harry and Meghan, I am not convinced brother Prince William will be so forgiving.”

He added: “It would take a great act of forgiveness and I’m not sure Wills is ready to do that.”

Harry and Meghan made a string of claims which caused deep hurt to William and Catherine, who has also endured her own cancer ordeal.



Harry’s comments about Camilla were also particularly damaging.

In Spare, he described her as “the villain” and “dangerous”, and alleged she sacrificed him on her “personal PR altar” and leaked private family conversations.

Edwards points out that Harry made millions from the book.

Camilla, he believes, is likely to support the King if he wants to give his son a second chance, though William could be a different story.

The brothers were once at the heart of the so-called Fab Four alongside their wives, but the relationship has since spectacularly broken down.



Where will Archie and Lilibet go to school?

The Sussexes have refused to reveal where their children will be educated, citing privacy and security reasons.

Archie is now at prep-school age, while Lilibet is eligible for Year One.

Reports that Archie had been registered for Eton were previously denied by sources close to the Sussexes.



Prince William’s eldest son George, 13, is due to start at the prestigious school next month.

The Sussexes’ decision to educate their children in Britain is nevertheless a major change after years of raising them in California.

The Duke of Sussex spoke positively in memoir Spare about his own first school, Ludgrove.

The all-boys school costs £14,477 per term.

But it is boarding-only, and he talked about it being hard to live in a place where many boys “lived in close proximity”.



The Sussexes have denied suggestions Harry has registered Archie for Eton, which takes boys from 13.

He lamented his own time at the school in his book.

It comes as…

Where will Harry and Meghan live?

Their new home is also being kept secret, but what is known is that it will not be a royal property.



The couple have been without a UK home for four-and-a-half years, after Charles evicted them from Frogmore Cottage in January 2023 following the publication of Spare.

The Cotswolds is popular with American celebrities and A listers who want to live discreetly, and it is near to the King’s Highgrove Estate.

Former talk show host Ellen Degeneres had a property there and was friends with Meghan in California.

Meghan appeared on her talk show for her first sit-down daytime interview after moving to California in November 2021, and Harry and Meghan were guests at Ellen and Portia de Rossi’s vow renewal ceremony in February 2023.



And, in 2024 Ellen wrote online that the couple had taken in one of her rescue chickens.

There were, however, rumours of a tension between Meghan and Ellen after Ellen moved to the UK.

The Cotswolds would also be an attractive area for Meghan because of the nearby Soho Farmhouse.

Meghan is famously friends with exec Markus Anderson, often dubbed the “King of Soho House”.

He helped arrange discreet dates for her and Harry when they began dating, including at 76 Dean Street in London, and Soho Farmhouse in Oxfordshire.



But Prince Harry may want to be close to his mother Princess Diana’s childhood home at Althorp House in Northants where her grave is.

Also in July, he took his children on an emotional visit to Diana’s grave at the house.

Royals do, nevertheless, often choose to live in peaceful Windsor.

The Sussexes will retain their £11million Montecito mansion and Portugal bolthole.

What will they do for work?

Meghan has made no secret of her love of the Hollywood spotlight since moving to California.



She has regularly appeared at glitzy awards shows, red-carpet events and celebrity gatherings, while building her own lifestyle brand and media projects.

But now she is moving back to Britain, that world is rather different.

But questions remain over what else she will do with her time in Britain, as she currently has no UK-based projects or campaigns publicly announced.



So will we start seeing Meghan at the UK’s biggest celebrity events? Could she turn up at Wimbledon, film premieres, fashion events or star-studded red carpets?

The Sussexes have repeatedly stressed their desire for privacy, particularly when it comes to Archie and Lilibet.

But Meghan has also shown she is perfectly comfortable stepping into the limelight when it suits her.

Her return therefore raises an obvious question over whether she will divide her time between a private family life and the British celebrity circuit.

There could also be a new role for her on the charity scene.



Meghan has previously backed causes including women’s empowerment and girls’ education, while Harry remains heavily involved with his own charitable work.

And if the couple do begin attending high-profile events, it will inevitably raise another question: where does the line sit between their private life and their relationship with the Royal Family?

Harry is expected to continue his charity work, including his links to WellChild and the Invictus Games.

He is due to return to Britain in September for patronages including the WellChild Awards.

Will they push for the half-in, half-out role they always wanted?

For now, there is no suggestion Harry and Meghan are being restored as working royals.



But their return inevitably brings back one of the biggest arguments at the heart of Megxit.

The couple originally wanted a “half-in, half-out” arrangement, allowing them to support the Queen while also becoming financially independent.

The late Queen Elizabeth II ultimately rejected that idea.



After the Sandringham summit in 2020, the Sussexes were stripped of their official roles and Harry lost his military appointments.

They went on to build their commercial life in America, signing major deals and developing their own brands.

But now Harry is returning to Britain, his father is King and the pair appear to have begun rebuilding their relationship.

That inevitably raises the question of whether the old rules could ever be revisited.

Could Charles be more willing to find a compromise with his son than his mother was?



The King is understood to welcome the chance to see more of Harry and his grandchildren, and any future discussion over a role would have to take place between father and son.

But there is a huge obstacle.

Harry and Meghan still intend to run their private businesses, while the Royal Family has already made clear that working royals cannot simply pick and choose when they are “in” and “out”.

For now, sources insist there is no new royal role on the table.

But if this return marks the beginning of a genuine reconciliation between Harry and his father, the question of what comes next is unlikely to disappear.



Will they start attending royal events?

With Harry and Meghan now expected to spend far more time in Britain, attention will inevitably turn to major family occasions.

Could they appear at Christmas at Sandringham? Could Harry attend Remembrance events again?

And could Meghan eventually stand alongside other members of the Royal Family at public occasions?



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Nothing has been confirmed.

The King is understood to want more private family time with his grandchildren, but there is no indication that the Sussexes are being brought back into the official royal fold.

News.title: Mum-to-be, 23, battered two nurses and told one ‘you are dead’ after they tried to stop her fleeing appointment
News.content:
HOSPITAL ATTACK Mum-to-be, 23, battered two nurses and told one ‘you are dead’ after they tried to stop her fleeing appointment

A MUM-to-be battered two nurses who tried to stop her fleeing a hospital appointment, a court heard.

Jessica Pollitt attacked Laura Bellamy and Gemma Tang when she “shot up” off a bed while being examined at a mental health unit in Southport.



The 23-year-old ran outside into the street as the nurses attempted to coax her back to the hospital.

But Pollitt launched into the attack – punching both Laura and Gemma as they tried to restrain her.



After she was taken to a seclusion unit, she told Gemma: “Wait till I am out of this. You are dead.”

Pollitt, who is 21 weeks pregnant, broke down as she admitted four charges of common assault.



She was sentenced to a 12-month community order with a requirement that she attends up to 20 days of rehabilitation activity.

Sefton Magistrates’ Court was told the assault took place on December 27 last year when Pollitt was staying at a mental health inpatient unit at Ormskirk district hospital.

She had been admitted to a facility at Southport for an appointment but was described as “agitated”.

Prosecutor Teri O’Brien said: “Whilst at the hospital the doctor treating the defendant briefly left the room whereupon she suddenly shot up off the hospital bed and exited at a fast walking pace.



“She was persuaded to come back and proceeded to go and run away. The instructions were to keep her in sight and communicate to prevent any further harm but there were concerns as she approached a main road.

”She made verbal threats, ‘If you do not stop following me I will batter you.’ Then as Laura Bellamy was on the phone to police, the defendant heard her, turned around and ran directly at her and the other colleague Gemma Tang.

“As the defendant has approached Laura Bellamy and her colleague she began to punch out and physically assault Laura Bellamy and repeatedly assault her to the face.



“When Ms Bellamy tried to defend herself she took numerous strikes to wrists and arms. Gemma Tang bear-hugged the defendant from behind to restrict her arm movements to assist her colleague – but the defendant managed to turn around and swing punches at her.

”Most have missed but she landed numerous times on her arm. Both victims then withdrew due to the danger at the time. Police attended and proceeded to search for the defendant and located her at a bus stop.”

The court heard Pollitt, who has autism, was taken to a seclusion unit at Chorley but had another outburst towards Laura and pinned her to the wall.

Ms O’Brien said: “These offences are aggravated by the fact they were committed on two people providing a public service.”

In mitigation for Pollitt who now stays at a wellbeing centre in Preston, defence solicitor Grahame Halliwell said she was “extremely distressed”.



He told the court both nurses suffered “reddening” but “nothing more serious”.

Mr Halliwell added: “Both victims use the words that this was ‘incredibly out of character’ for the defendant.

“She has been candid and cooperative over what happened and has expressed remorse. “

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Pollitt was also fined £180 and ordered to pay £133 in costs and surcharge.

JP James Long told her: ”The bench wishes you all the best moving forward. Hopefully, this can be a turning point for you.”

News.title: Seven symptoms to watch out for as popular dog food is urgently recalled in UK after pets ‘lose their sight’
News.content:
PET owners have been warned to look out for seven symptoms after a popular dog food is recalled.

The premium brand has warned customers not to feed the meals to “any animal”.



Fresh dog food company Years has temporarily paused all subscriptions after their buckwheat-based meals were found to be potentially linked with eye reactions in pets.

Around 57 dogs have developed symptoms of keratoconjunctivitis sicca, known as bilateral dry eye, after consuming the wholefood products, according to reports from the Press Association.



The brand has launched a formal investigation into the signature meals after reports that some pets have lost their sight.

A Years spokesperson urged shoppers to “stop feeding Years fresh meals immediately, whether your dog is experiencing symptoms or not”.



The company has advised customers to look out for a number of symptoms, including:

Red, irritated or swollen eyes

Excessive blinking or squinting

Cloudy or dull eye surfaces

A thick sticky mucus discharge

Corneal ulcers

Pawing at the eyes

Eyes may take on a blue-ish tinge

Pet owners who notice any of the above symptoms in their animal after consuming the subscription meals have been urged to contact the Years support team.

Years confirmed it is reformulating its products to remove buckwheat, leading to subscriptions to be stopped for a precautionary six weeks.

It asked for the meals not be donated or sold, and has offered free collection of any unused food with full credit offered in exchange.



A spokesman for Years previously said: “We’re sorry for the worry and disruption this will cause – both for the dogs affected and to all of our customers.”

News.title: 'Doctors told me I was infertile - then I took a pregnancy test'
News.content:
'Doctors told me I was infertile - then I took a pregnancy test'

Shannon Maya Lamb was told she could not fall pregnant again after battling cancer while pregnant with her son, Hunter

View 6 Images Shannon and her first child (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

A mum who was diagnosed with ovarian cancer while pregnant with her first child and told chemotherapy would leave her infertile has just given birth to her second 'miracle' baby. Shannon Maya Lamb, 31, was diagnosed with aggressive ovarian cancer in October 2020, after spotting a lump on her pelvis while lying in the bath.

‌



She had invasive surgery to remove the tumour and discovered she was pregnant with her first child in March 2022. But the news came weeks after learning her ovarian cancer had already spread to her lung, and she needed surgery to remove a portion of it.

‌



When a CT scan revealed at 31 weeks pregnant that there was further disease in a 4cm lymph node beside her lung, she needed emergency chemotherapy and an emergency caesarean section to deliver her premature son, Hunter, who is now three.

‌



What followed were 11 further rounds of aggressive chemotherapy and two stem cell transplants. In October 2024, she was confirmed to be in remission - but due to the life-saving cancer treatments, she was told she could not fall pregnant again.

View 6 Images Shannon was diagnosed with ovarian cancer while pregnant with her first child (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

But in November 2025, she got sore breasts and a period - and discovered she had fallen pregnant again. Single mum Shannon, who is now over two years cancer free, was delighted to learn she was expecting a healthy baby girl, who was born last month.

‌



Biomedical science student Shannon, from Dundee, who spoke to Talk to the Press, said: "I remember first noticing this lump on the side of my pelvis, and my hair began to thin.

"I first questioned if it was a hernia but it ended up causing the worst pain I'd ever felt. It was aggressive cancer and I had surgery all alone because of Covid. But in early 2022 I got shortness of breath and I found out there was a 'suspicious' nodule in my lung, the same week I learned I was pregnant.

Dr Amir Khan shares 'end-of-the-bed' test GPs do on every patient READ MORE :

"I had surgery at 16 weeks pregnant, but the cancer had already spread. I had Hunter at 31 weeks and went down to the chemo unit four days later. I needed to say alive for my son, I'd have given up without him.

‌



"I was told I would be infertile after the stem cell transplants - I just had to accept it. So it's a miracle I'm here, my son is here, and I have my miracle baby daughter too."

Shannon was first diagnosed with germ cell ovarian cancer after spotting a lump on her abdomen, which grew within a matter of weeks. She said: "I had been lying in the bath. It was hard, and my friend suggested it might a hernia. I didn't know what was wrong."

She was referred to gynaecology and it was confirmed to be a 14cm by 13cm cancerous tumour on her left ovary. On December 22, she underwent surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary to remove the infected ovary and surrounding affected areas.

‌



From then, she was discharged and given regular scans as it was believed to have removed all the cancer. She was thrilled to learn she had fallen pregnant in April 2022.

However, around the same time, Shannon began suffering with shortness of breath, fatigue, aching joints and weight loss. A chest x-ray revealed a 'suspicious shadow' on her lung - which biopsies later revealed were a relapse.

View 6 Images Shannon was told chemo would leave her infertile (Image: SWNS)

‌



At 16 weeks, Shannon had a surgery to remove the bottom lobe of her right lung, which contained five tumours. But at 29 weeks pregnant, a CT scan revealed the cancer had already spread and there were tumours on her lymph node, spine, coccyx, left pelvic bone and by her kidney.

Shannon said: "I started chemotherapy at 31 weeks and gave birth to Hunter just after that. Four days after my emergency c-section I was back having more chemotherapy.

"I just wanted to be with my baby, but I couldn't. I had to FaceTime him with the nurses. When I could finally see him, it was only for 30 minutes a day when I was disconnected from the chemo, and I had to wear gloves."

‌



View 6 Images Shannon spotted a lump on her pelvis while lying in the bath (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

Shannon spent the following months having 11 rounds of chemotherapy, and then two stem cell transplants with high-dose chemo. Throughout the course of the stem cell transplants, Shannon caught sepsis twice, and feared at points she would not survive.

By August 2023, the treatment was over, and a surgery in October 2024 to remove bones in her spine to test for cancer revealed it was gone, and had been in remission since July 2023. She has now been in remission for three years.

‌



But she was warned before the chemotherapy and stem cell transplants that eradicating the cancer would cost her her fertility. Shannon said: "Especially with one ovary, I was told the chance of recovering ovary function was pretty much nil.

"I was deemed infertile and menopausal, and prescribed hormone replacement therapy (HRT). But in July 2025, I began questioning my fertility - I was still having period-like bleeds.

"I requested blood checks, which confirmed I was post-menopausal - and two pregnancy tests came back negative. I thought, 'this is stupid, I'm clearly infertile' but decided to do a digital test anyway. I was confident it would be negative - until it said, 'pregnant'."

‌



View 6 Images Shannon has just given birth to her second 'miracle' baby (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

Incredibly, Shannon was indeed expecting a baby girl – and miracle baby Zayla was born via c-section on July 22. Shannon had some complications and was hospitalised after her bowel became obstructed in the weeks leading up to the birth, and Zayla suffered with three bouts of jaundice shortly after birth.

But now the family are all happy, healthy and safe at home and Shannon is loving being a mum-of-two. She said: "During treatment, I was on death's door. I would never have imagined now I'd have a healthy little boy and a little girl.

‌



"I'm meant to be infertile! My friend joked I must just have a really strong ovary. I'm being monitored but as far as we are aware, I'm still completely cancer free.

View 6 Images Shannon and her second child (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

"The whole thing has been miraculous - unbelievable and a blessing. I'm grateful to have been given a second chance at life, and my little girl is a miracle.

Article continues below

“I look at her and I’m so in love, I can’t find the words to describe it. I’m so blessed to have both my daughter and my son. I’m so, so lucky.

"I hope my story might give others hope - when there doesn't seem like there can be a happy ending, there might still be one anyway."

News.title: 'Much-loved' grandad, 77, dies after being hit by vehicle in Aldi car park
News.content:
'Much-loved' grandad, 77, dies after being hit by vehicle in Aldi car park

David Bush, 77, died in hospital after being hit by a Toyota Prius in an Aldi car park in Brighouse, West Yorkshire.

View 2 Images David Bush died in hospital after being hit by a car in an Aldi car park in Brighouse, West Yorkshire. (Image: YORKSHIRE LIVE/MEN MEDIA)

A “much-loved” grandad has died in hospital nearly two weeks after being hit by a vehicle in an Aldi car park.

‌



David Bush was hit by a Toyota Prius in the supermarket car park on Halifax Road in Brighouse, West Yorkshire, at around 12.55pm on August 6.

‌



The 77-year-old suffered serious, life-threatening injuries and died in hospital on August 17.

‌



His family have since paid an emotional tribute, saying he would be “missed dearly”. They said: “David was a much-loved husband, father, and grandfather and will be missed dearly by those knew him.”

View 2 Images Police on the scene at the Aldi car park on Halifax Road in Brighouse. (Image: Newsquest / SWNS)

‌



A 46-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and has since been bailed pending further enquiries.

Officers from West Yorkshire Police ’s Major Collision Enquiry Team are investigating and want to hear from anyone who witnessed the collision.

Police are also appealing for anyone who may have dash-cam footage of the incident to come forward.

Article continues below

Anyone with information can contact West Yorkshire Police via its Live Chat service, quoting log 696 of August 6, or speak anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Thousands of students celebrate GCSE results day - but regional divide widens
News.content:
Thousands of students celebrate GCSE results day - but regional divide widens

More than a fifth (22.0%) of UK entries were awarded the top grades - at least a 7 or an A grade - this year, up by 0.1 percentage points on last year, when 21.9% achieved the top grades

View 3 Images Students open their results at Llanishen High School in Cardiff, Wales (Image: Getty Images)

Hundreds of thousands of teens celebrate GCSE results today as the proportion of entries awarded top grades has risen from last year.

‌



More than a fifth (22.0%) of UK entries were awarded the top grades - at least a 7 or an A grade - this year, up by 0.1 percentage points on last year, when 21.9% achieved the top grades.

‌



But national figures also showed the rate scoring a decent pass returned to pre-pandemic levels. Some 67.3% of GCSE entries scored at least a 4 or a C grade – considered a “standard pass” – down from 67.4% in 2025 and the same as in 2019.

‌



Many of the pupils who are receiving their GCSE results this summer were in Year 5 - aged nine of 10 - when schools closed because of Covid-19, meaning their secondary education was not disrupted by the height of the pandemic.

The gap in results between boys and girls also shrunk again, and is at its narrowest point this century. But the regional gap widened, with top grades between London, the best performing region, and the North East, the worst performing, widening to a record high of 10.9 percentage points, up from 10.6 last year. It is the largest gap since the start of available data in 2010.

Students celebrate A-level results day after record number accepted on degree courses READ MORE :

View 3 Images Education Secretary Lucy Powell speaks with students collecting their GCSE results at Harper Green School in Farnworth, Bolton (Image: Peter Byrne/PA Wire)

‌



The Department for Education on Thursday said ministers are committed to tackling "entrenched inequality, so that where you are born does not determine what you go on to achieve".

It pointed to the Government's Regional Improvement for Standards and Excellence (RISE) teams that work with the schools and areas where performance is weakest and its Mission North East and Mission Coastal to improve outcomes in some of our most deprived areas.

PM Andy Burnham has vowed to offer more technical routes for teenagers to improve career opportunities across the country. In one of his first acts as PM, he announced that from next year, Year 10 pupils will be able to combine core academic subjects, like English and Maths, with technical education linked to jobs available in their area.

‌



On Thursday, he said: "Congratulations to everyone getting their GCSE results today, you should be proud of the work that got you here. Whatever your results, remember there isn't just one route to success. We're creating more opportunities for young people to choose the path that's right for them, whether that's academic or technical. Every young person should have the chance to fulfil their potential. I'll make sure they do."

Education Secretary Lucy Powell also promised to crack down on the "conveyor belt" of resits teenagers face if they fail to secure at least a grade 4 in English and/or maths GCSE. She said repeated resits lead to us “branding (students) as a failure” and affecting self-confidence.

She told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “That’s why we’re going to be looking at that, and I’m going to be bringing in a new stepping stone qualification, as we’re calling it, a level one… in maths and in English, so that there is an additional qualification that young people can work towards.

‌



"And I want to work with employers to make sure that that qualification is credible, is respected, and that employers see that as sufficient or more than sufficient for young people to go on to do things like an apprenticeship in construction or health and social care."

View 3 Images National figures showed the rate scoring a decent pass returned to pre-pandemic levels (Image: Newcastle Chronicle)

On regional disparities, Lee Elliot Major, professor of social mobility at the University of Exeter, said: “It is a damning indictment of 21st-century Britain that where you happen to grow up has such a profound impact on your educational and life chances.

‌



“Something is fundamentally amiss when children with the same talents and potential face such different prospects simply because of where they happen to live. England’s educational divide is a story of London increasingly pulling away from much of the rest of the country.

“But these broad regional divides conceal an even more troubling geography of opportunity: sometimes a few streets, or a different postcode, can make the difference between a life of opportunity and a life of overlooked talent.”

On the gender gap, the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys (CPRMB) said the disparities at GCSE level, and in education more widely, can mean boys struggle to thrive after leaving school.

‌



Overall, nearly a quarter (24.4%) of girls’ GCSE entries were awarded at least a grade 7/A compared with almost a fifth of boys’ entries (19.6%) - a 4.8 percentage point gap, down from a difference of 5.1 last year. Meanwhile, 70.2% of girls’ GCSE entries were awarded at least a grade 4/C compared with 64.4% of boys’ entries – a 5.8 percentage point gap, a decrease from 6.2 last year.

CPRMB research officer Martha Lucas said: “For a lot of employment, meeting that grade four in maths and English is a barrier to finding that employment. This year, the number of male Neets (not in education, employment or training) hit more than 500,000.

“So, boys are consistently leaving school without the qualifications nor education necessary for them to thrive in adult life – get a job, be in employment – and quite frankly that desperately needs to change.”

Article continues below

The figures, published by the Joint Council for Qualifications (JCQ), cover GCSE entries from students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. A 4 is broadly equivalent to a C grade and a 7 is broadly equivalent to an A.

News.title: King Charles 'blindsided' by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's bombshell UK return
News.content:
King Charles 'blindsided' by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's bombshell UK return

Royal sources say the King only found out about Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's plans to return to the UK with their children, who will attend school in Britain, on Sunday

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle set to move back to UK

The King has been blindsided by Prince Harry and Meghan’s bombshell plans to move back to the UK - and was only told about them three days ago, royal sources have said.

‌



The Sussexes are returning to the UK later this month – making their home in a non-royal residence outside of London – and have already enrolled Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet in British schools. It is understood Harry and Meghan's plans would have been months in the making, however the King, who has had a rocky relationship with his younger son, was only made aware of the move on Sunday.

‌



He was not told about it when he met H arry, Meghan and their children at Highgrove on their trip to the UK last month with the move coming just a year after the Duke of Sussex said his security in the UK made it 'impossible' for his family to visit.

‌



Harry and Meghan to move back to UK in weeks with Archie and Lilibet to attend school READ MORE :

View 4 Images The King is said to have learned of Harry and Meghan's plans on Sunday (Image: PA)

A royal source said: "The King and the entire royal family have undoubtedly been blindsided by the announcement from Harry and Meghan that they are returning to the UK.

"After saying that he could not see a situation safe enough to bring his wife and children to the UK just over a year ago, the fact Prince Harry is now fully prepared to not only visit but live in the country he left behind is extraordinary.

‌



"While the King will be delighted at the prospect at seeing his grandchildren on a more regular basis, there will be concerns over the true motivation for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's decision to leave the United States after everything that has occurred since they decided to leave their royal roles.

"It is without question that the hybrid roles Harry and Meghan wanted before choosing to leave their royal roles behind will not be offered, which poses more questions as to what public role they will seek to carve out in the UK."

‌



The Sussexes’ decision also raises the question of how the news will be met by the Prince and Princess of Wales . William – a future kin g – is estranged from his brother after Harry levelled a barrage of accusations against the prince, Kate, the King and Queen Camilla in the years since the Megxit crisis of 2020.

Harry and Meghan’s status as non-working members of the Royal Family will remain the same, with the couple not being offered a “half-in-half-out” option when it comes to their roles.

They are expected to remain financially independent and continue their commercial and charitable work, while Harry is not expected to undertake official royal duties. They are retaining their home in Montecito, California as well as their holiday home in Portugal.

‌



View 4 Images Prince Harry and Meghan with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

The news also comes weeks after the family visited the UK together for the first time in four years last month, where as well as meeting the King, they stayed with Harry's uncle Earl Spencer at Althorp, where Harry's late mother Princess Diana is buried.

However, the decision is particularly striking given Harry's previous concerns about bringing his family back to Britain as he does not automatically get taxpayer-funded security while in the UK.

‌



The Duke has spent years challenging the decision in the courts over his security arrangements after losing the protection when he ceased to be a working royal and moved overseas.

Just last year, Harry even told the BBC in an interview that without such security, he "can't see a world in which I would be bringing my wife and children back to the UK at this point".

His return could therefore reignite questions over what security arrangements will be put in place for the Sussexes and who would pay for them. Despite making millions since leaving his role as a working royal in 2020, and arranging his own private security team, Harry has claimed he remains a target for terrorists in the UK and needs protection from the Metropolitan Police when he returns..

‌



View 4 Images Prince Harry during a public appearance in Washington DC yesterday (Image: AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

The Home Office has always maintained that Harry’s security is considered on a case-by-case basis if he informs the department of his travel plans at least 28 days in advance. Dai Davies, former the head of Scotland Yard's Royal Protection Command, said the bill to secure Sussexes’ new home would prove costly.

He told Sky News: “If they go somewhere new, that place would have to be reconnoitred, it would have to have technical support, a whole manner of things, including potentially a safe room.

‌



“It’s hugely expensive, and would take time. So it's very interesting where they're going to go, and that raises a number of questions in my mind - how long have they been preparing for this? Who has been helping them and so on, so forth?”

View 4 Images The Sussexes on their recent trip to Australia (Image: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP)

Earlier this month, the Mirror revealed how Harry is now so determined to reconcile with his family and that he won’t do anything to jeopardise it, as he places far greater importance on repairing family ties than at any point since he and his wife Meghan stepped back as working royals in 2020.

‌



Meanwhile, the decision is also a huge appears to be a huge U-turn for Meghan, who has only visited the UK once since the late Queen's funeral in 2022 and on her recent trip here, did not appear in public.

In an interview with The Cut in 2022, Meghan talked about her fears of sending her children to school in the UK claiming paparazzi would swarm her at the school gates.

She said: "Sorry, I have a problem with that. That doesn’t make me obsessed with privacy. That makes me a strong and good parent protecting my child.”

‌



And according the royal expert Jennie Bond, it appears the Duchess is "taking one for the team” by moving back to the UK with her family.

The former royal correspondent, who covered the royal family for 14 years with the BBC, told Sky News: “I think we should beware a pile-on on Meghan in particular, and I can see that already happening.

Article continues below

"This is the decision they’ve made probably for the sake of their children, as much as for Harry. Perhaps Meghan is taking one for the team here, because I’m not sure this is her life’s desire to live back in the UK.”

News.title: Professor Tim Spector issues bran flakes breakfast warning
News.content:
Professor Tim Spector issues bran flakes breakfast warning

It's eaten by millions every day - but food scientist warns that new research has come to a shocking conclusion

View Image Tim Spector gave a warning over a breakfast eaten by millions (Image: Zoe)

Professor Tim Spector has issued a warning about a breakfast eaten by millions - and which he himself ate every day. The Professor of Genetic Epidemiology at King’s College London and co-founder of the Zoe health app said that people should reconsider having low-fat milk and bran flakes - and change it up.

‌



Speaking on his Instagram page, Prof Spector explained that it is ‘complete rubbish’ - according to new science. He said: “15 years ago, this used to be my go-to breakfast cereal. Low-fat milk and low calorie bran flakes. I used to think this was great. And it was all about calories. But the latest science is telling us that is complete rubbish. This breakfast cereal will actually make you hungrier. It’s not filling you up. It’s not helping your gut microbes.”

‌



He explained in his post that the issue is that focusing on calories is the wrong way to approach food. He explained: “Cereal with skimmed milk might look light on paper, but because the natural fats have been stripped away from the milk, there is nothing in the bowl to slow down digestion. The refined grains and milk sugars can cause a blood sugar spike, followed by a slump. That sudden crash is precisely why you find yourself hunting for a snack a few hours later.”

‌



Instead, Prof Spector advised an option full of fat: “A bowl of full-fat Greek yoghurt with berries, nuts, and seeds works in the opposite way. The protein in the yoghurt and the fats in the nuts act like a brake on your stomach, forcing it to release food into your system slowly and steadily. This keeps your blood sugar steady while signalling directly to your brain that you’re full.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



“Add some berries on top for fibre and a good dose of polyphenols, the natural defence chemicals in plants that feed your gut microbes, and you’ll have a balanced breakfast that will support your energy and keep you satisfied until lunchtime.

“This bowl is completely different. It’s full of different diverse plants, high fiber, polyphenols, high fats, sending signals to your gut microbes which send signals to your brain to say, 'I’m no longer hungry.' So, the one lesson I’d love you to take away from this is that when you’re building your breakfast, which is probably the most important meal of the day that you can be in charge of, go for something that’s got good fats in it.

Prof Tim Spector's warning for anyone who ate a burger over the bank holiday READ MORE :

"It’s got plants, it’s got diversity, and feed your gut microbes. Importantly, you must always favor quality over calories.”

Article continues below

His followers agreed with one saying: "Yes! A yoghurt bowl with berries, nuts, and seeds is my go to" Another added: "Yes I have a daily Greek yoghurt bowl - blueberries, oats and dark chocolate are my go-to combo."

Manchester Pride Fringe 2026: Full programme, dates, venues and how to go

Manchester Village Pride returns 28–31 August 2026 after uncertainty in 2025. Here’s the Pride Fringe programme, tickets info, venues and what’s on across the Gay Village

View 2 Images Here's everything you need to know about this month's pride events in Manchester

Manchester Village Pride returns on Friday, 28 August 2026, after facing uncertainty following the collapse of the event’s previous organiser in late 2025. Organisers said there was a “real risk that our city’s cornerstone celebration would disappear.”

In response, business owners, residents and activists from the Gay Village formed Manchester Village Pride CIC to keep the celebrations going. The community-run weekend is back from 28th to 31st August, alongside a Pride Fringe of independent events, screenings, tours and parties across one of the world’s leading LGBTQ+ cities.

News.title: Parents facing postcode lottery for school uniform help as only 22 councils in England offer grants
News.content:
Parents facing postcode lottery for school uniform help as only 22 councils in England offer grants

The average cost of a secondary school uniform is now an estimated £442 - and while there is help available for some families, it all depends on where you live

View 2 Images School uniform can be a hefty expensive for parents (stock image) (Image: JohnnyGreig via Getty Images)

Families struggling with the cost of school uniforms are facing a postcode lottery for financial help.

‌



School uniform grants are provided by all councils in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland - but it is not a statutory requirement in England. This means councils in England are not required by law to offer support. For the councils that do provide help, the eligibility criteria also varies widely, but normally you need to be on a low income or claiming benefits.

‌



New analysis by free money advice service Money Wellness found that only 22 local authorities in England offer a school uniform grant, while a further seven only provide help in exceptional circumstances. You can find a full list of councils that still offer school uniform grants below.

‌



View 2 Images The average cost of a secondary school uniform is now an estimated £442 (Image: Getty Images)

Almost half of parents are unaware of new September school uniform rule - it could save you money READ MORE :

Money Wellness reviewed all 153 local councils in England. If a local authority does not offer support, residents may be able to get help through the Government's Crisis and Resilience Fund instead. The average cost of a secondary school uniform is now an estimated £442, while primary school uniform costs £343.

‌



Research by The Children's Society found that 38% of parents struggled with uniform costs last year. The findings come as separate Money Wellness research found that almost half (48%) of parents were unaware that primary schools in England will only be able to require a maximum of three branded uniform items from September 2026. Secondary schools can require up to four items if one of them is a tie.

Adam Rolfe, Policy and Public Affairs Officer at Money Wellness, said: “For many families, buying school uniform is one of the biggest expenses of the year, yet the help available depends almost entirely on your postcode. Some councils offer dedicated school uniform grants, others provide support through local welfare schemes, while in many areas families may not realise help is available unless they actively look for it.

Article continues below

"If you're worried about the cost of uniforms, don't assume there's no support. Even if your council no longer offers a dedicated school uniform grant, you may still be able to get help through its Crisis and Resilience Fund or other local welfare assistance schemes. It's always worth checking before turning to borrowing."
