World.title: Raiders of the Cookie Jar: Harrison Ford and Cookie Monster break the internet
World.content:
Need some cheering up? Considering the current state of the world, we don’t blame you.

 

Well, brace yourselves for a clip which has broken the internet. In the best of ways.

Acting legend Harrison Ford has teamed up with Sesame Street’s very own Cookie Monster and the pair ended up singing the Indiana Jones theme tune. Whilst munching on cookies, naturally.

“Me think me know this song,” said the Cookie Monster as he began humming John Williams’ iconic composition. This led the usually grumpy 84-year-old actor to break the cantankerous act and join in.

The behind-the-scenes clip, taken when Ford appeared on the show earlier this year, was shared online by the furry blue Muppet with a crippling addiction for baked goods (preferably with chocolate chips). It has gone viral and racked up 2.5 million views, as well as rave reviews.

Check it out below:

“This is so wholesome it gave me the feels,” wrote one user on X, while another commented: “Harrison Ford breaking his grumpy old man character and just having fun is always so great.”

“This has made my month,” added one user. Another declared: “This is genuinely one of the greatest things ever recorded.”

Maybe... Although we won't be satisfied until this batch made in heaven pairs up once more for a rendition of Rihanna's 'S&M' with the reworked lyric: "Whips and dough excite me"...

Is that too munch to ask? (Sorry.)

Elsewhere, it’s been a good week for Indiana Jones fans, as Disney recently announced that Ford would be donning the fedora and whip again in a new project. Not a cinematic one though, as Ford will participate in the new ride at Disney World’s Animal Kingdom park.

Ford revealed to fans in a pre-taped video message that he is the “actual model” for the animatronic robot featured on Indiana Jones and the Myth of the Jade Serpent, which is currently under construction.

“I’m excited for you to see his next epic adventure,” the Oscar-nominated actor said. “I’m coming to Walt Disney World soon.”

This project marks the first time that Ford’s likeness will be used in an Indiana Jones attraction at the Disney parks. It is unclear if he will lend his voice to the ride.

A specific opening date for the ride has not yet been announced.

Ford played Indiana Jones for the first time in 1981’s Raiders of the Lost Ark, which was followed by Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (1984) and Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989).

After a lengthy hiatus, Ford returned to the beloved role in 2008 with Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull and in 2023 with Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny. Sadly, the latter was a critical and commercial flop for Disney and Lucasfilm, ending his tenure on a bum note.

There have been rumours that the long-running franchise could be coming back to the big screen in a rebooted version, but these rumblings were shut down earlier this year by Lucasfilm chief Kathleen Kennedy. She told Deadline in an interview that reviving the series is highly unlikely.

“I don’t think Indy will ever be done, but I don’t think anybody is interested right now in exploring it,” she said.

For the time being, we have Indy chomping on cookies. And that’s more than enough.

Ford’s last big screen role to date was in Captain America: Brave New World, in which he played President Thaddeus Ross / Red Hulk. He currently stars as Dr. Paul Rhoades in the acclaimed comedy-drama TV show Shrinking, which was renewed for a fourth season in January.

World.title: Overcome market fragmentation or miss the AI train, Lagarde warns the EU
World.content:
Europe missed the first digital revolution and cannot afford to miss out again with AI, as it has the full potential to compete, Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), said on Wednesday.

 

To win the AI race against giants such as the US and China, Lagarde told the International Business Council of the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Geneva, the EU needs to complete its single market and integrate capital markets that remain too fragmented.

"Europe largely missed out on the first digital revolution, as the commercial gains from the spread of information and communication technologies were captured disproportionately elsewhere. We cannot afford to repeat that experience with artificial intelligence (AI), the second digital revolution," she said in Geneva.

Lagarde's analysis largely echoes that of her predecessor, Mario Draghi, who in 2024 delivered a seminal report on relaunching the EU's economic competitiveness, which pointed to AI as the last chance for Europe to rejoin the international tech race.

Following Draghi's advice, the European Commission has put forward several initiatives to promote the uptake of AI in strategic sectors as well as the financing of massive data centres in an effort to develop new generations of the technology.

In her speech, Lagarde stressed that access to capital is limiting Europe's AI investments, notably because EU businesses get most of their funding through bank credit, while capital markets — the spaces where investors invest and firms raise capital — remain too limited at the national level.

Legal fragmentation creates practical barriers for firms in terms of costs, timings and their ability to operate across borders, she said. As a result, a company in Europe faces more hurdles to scale up than a US-based rival, and may end up turning to non-EU capital markets to solve the problem.

"Scale is particularly important as new technologies reshape the sources of productivity growth," Lagarde said.

The president added that Europe has the full potential to "make the most of new technologies", and that there are already "encouraging signs that European firms are investing in AI".

"The EU accounts for around 6% of the world's population but as many as 15% of its researchers. It also produces almost one-fifth of the world's most-cited scientific publications," the ECB president pointed out.

"Survey evidence suggests that firms in the euro area expect to allocate an average of around 9% of their total investment to AI this year," Lagarde said.

The challenge, she argued, is turning this knowledge into "commercial success" that spreads the technology across the economy. "Too often, the barriers that prevent firms from scaling also hold back that diffusion," she added.

The ECB president called for speeding up key reforms currently under negotiation in Brussels, namely the Savings and Investment Union (SIU) and single market integration reforms such as EU Inc.

The SIU is a package of legislation aimed at creating more integrated capital markets. Legislators hope to reach a deal by the end of the year, though significant divisions remain among EU member states, particularly over reform of the centralised supervision of capital markets.

EU Inc. is the Commission's proposal for an optional, EU-wide company structure designed to make it faster and cheaper for firms — especially startups — to incorporate and operate across borders and grow, sidestepping the current patchwork of 27 national systems. This file, too, falls under the single market integration umbrella and is expected to be approved by the end of the year.

World.title: Banderol, Russia’s new low-cost weapon testing Ukraine’s air defences
World.content:
Russia deployed Banderol munitions in its overnight large-scale attack on Ukraine on Thursday, in what has become Moscow’s growing use of a low-cost weapon designed to overwhelm Ukraine's air defences.

 

Ukraine’s Air Force said the Banderols were intercepted during a barrage that also included cruise missiles and Shahed-type drones.

First recorded in Ukraine in spring 2025, the Banderol has become an increasingly common weapon of Russian attacks.

Also known as the S8000, it is a small jet-powered loitering munition that combines features of a cruise missile and a jet-powered attack drone.

It is considerably cheaper and carries a smaller warhead than a conventional cruise missile, but can require many of the same sophisticated air-defence systems to bring it down.

That imbalance is what makes the weapon particularly troublesome for Ukraine. Russia can produce and launch Banderols relatively cheaply while forcing Kyiv to commit scarcer and potentially more costly resources to intercept them.

Cheap weapon, expensive problem

The way the Banderol is launched adds to the challenge it poses. Unlike cruise missiles fired from strategic bombers, its use does not require the deployment of aircraft, whose take-off can give Ukrainian forces additional warning of an impending attack.

Manufactured by Russia’s UAV maker Kronshtadt JSC, the Banderol is primarily launched from Orion reconnaissance drones manufactured at the same plant, but has also been integrated into Mi-28 helicopters.

It can travel at more than 500km/h and has a range of up to 500km.

Because of the limited range, Moscow forces are launching Banderol’s from Russian-occupied Crimea towards the Odesa region.

Ukraine's Presidential envoy for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk said these missiles are involved in around 80% of Russian attacks on Odesa's infrastructure.

The weapon carries a 114kg fragmentation warhead containing up to 50kg of explosives. That is substantially smaller than the payloads of Russia’s Kh-101 and Iskander-K cruise missiles, which can carry warheads weighing roughly 400kg to 500kg.

But the Banderol’s significance lies less in its destructive power than in the economics of defending against it.

A Russian cruise missile can cost about €685,000 to produce, while the Banderol is estimated to cost between €42,500 and €127,500 depending on the components used.

That puts it broadly in the same price range as the Iranian-designed Shahed, one of the cheapest and most widely used weapons in Russia’s mass aerial attacks on Ukraine since 2022.

But the two pose different challenges for Ukrainian air defences. Shahed-type drones can increasingly be targeted with relatively inexpensive interceptor drones.

The faster Banderol requires more capable short- and mid-range air defence systems designed to counter cruise missiles, as well as MANPADS or fighter aircraft.

Russia may therefore be able to use Banderols not only to strike targets but to stretch the Ukrainian systems responsible for defending against more powerful cruise missiles.

The weapon relies on satellite navigation for guidance and can be disrupted by electronic warfare, but it also has an autonomous navigation system.

The Banderol also illustrates Russia’s continued ability to obtain foreign technology for its weapons industry despite Western sanctions and export restrictions imposed over the war.

According to Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR, the weapon contains a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and predominantly US-made electronic components.

World.title: “I wanna try it so bad”: How TikTok shapes what teenagers eat — and the role parents can play
World.content:
TikTok is becoming a double-edged source of nutrition advice for teenagers: the platform can offer recipes, cooking ideas and healthier alternatives, while also exposing young people to dieting culture, unrealistic body ideals and potentially misleading health claims. That creates a complicated environment for adolescents still developing their relationship with food, health and their bodies.

 

A recent study of teenagers aged 15 to 16 found that food content on TikTok could trigger cravings, encourage young people to try new foods and, in some cases, influence how they eat in an attempt to emulate influencers.

"Adolescents described TikTok as a highly engaging environment where food content can quickly capture their attention and cue a desire to eat or try something new," said an author of the study, Adrianna N. Bell.

The findings come as policymakers and courts take a closer look at the impact of social media on children and young people.

Currently in the US, Meta is facing a legal challenge over allegations that it deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to be addictive for young users. In Europe, in the meantime, TikTok was accused of breaching the European Union's online content rules, exposing children to cyberbullying or contact from abusers, while some national governments are moving to impose bans on social media platforms, including TikTok, for children.

The TikTok research adds another dimension to that debate: what happens when social media does not just influence how teenagers feel, but what they want to eat?

“It makes me wanna try it”

The study examined how adolescents perceived TikTok’s influence on their eating and what role their parents played.

The teenagers described a food environment in which trends, adverts, recipes, restaurant reviews and influencer content could quickly turn curiosity into appetite.

Trending food was particularly powerful because it was new — and because everyone else appeared to be trying it.

“The reason why I want to [try the trending food] is because I’m like, ‘why do so many people want to do it, like what’s so good about it?’ so it makes me wanna try it,” one of the teenagers that participated in the research said.

Presentation mattered too. Attractive food, professionally produced videos and positive comments could encourage cravings. Teenagers also said they took comments into account when deciding whether to trust a recommendation.

Influencers were another important part of the equation.

One participant described changing their diet after watching an influencer with a muscular physique:

“So, sometimes I be changing the way I eat. Because I’ve seen some dudes that are so buff and they have a good body you know and I’m like damn and so I click on his account and see what they’d be eating. And then I sometimes change how I eat, like to try to match it. ”

The influencer, therefore, does not necessarily need to be explicitly selling a food product. The message can instead be about a lifestyle — with food presented as part of the route towards a particular body or appearance.

When fast food starts to look normal

The study also highlights the role of TikTok’s algorithm.

Teenagers said their food choices could depend on what appeared on their personalised For You page. Repeated exposure could even affect how they perceived certain foods.

“I see so much fast food that like I don’t see fast food as unhealthy even though it is pretty unhealthy,” another participant said.

That reflects broader concerns about social media food marketing. Research has found that adolescents are frequently exposed to food adverts online and can be more attracted to social media advertising than traditional television advertising.

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis also found that celebrities and influencers promoting foods high in fat, sugar and salt can increase adolescents’ consumption of those foods.

On TikTok, however, advertising can be harder to separate from entertainment.

Food content can be a brand advert, an influencer recommendation, a restaurant review, a viral recipe or a creator simply joining a trend. The commercial message may be embedded within a video that looks like ordinary user-generated content.

And then there are the parents

Perhaps the most striking finding concerns what happens away from the screen.

Most teenagers said their parents played little or no role in their day-to-day TikTok use. But when parents did intervene, “they also described times when parents played an important role by interrupting exposure to food-related content and encouraging critical conversations about that content,” Bell said

Sometimes the intervention was not about TikTok at all. Family meals, spending time with siblings or simply having parents around could interrupt long periods of scrolling and reduce exposure to food-related content.

Other teenagers described a more direct form of parental influence: learning to question what they see online.

One participant said their mother had explained that influencers have different bodies and lifestyles, meaning that copying their diet would not necessarily produce the same results after she followed a diet seen on TikTok.

“… cause TikTok told me at a young age that, “do this [diet] and you’ll be skinny in 22 days” and I followed that the hard way,” a participant said.

That points towards a form of parental involvement that is less about surveillance and more about media literacy.

While the study is small and exploratory, involving 25 teenagers, the message is clear: TikTok is not simply showing teenagers what food looks like. It can shape what looks desirable, popular and normal.

And sometimes, as one teenager put it, that is enough to make them think: “I wanna try it so bad.”

World.title: Archaeologists uncover human offering at ancient ceremonial site in Lima
World.content:
Archaeologists in Peru have uncovered the skeletal remains of an adult believed to have been placed as a ritual offering more than 1,300 years ago.

 

The remains were discovered at Huaca Pucllana, a pre-Hispanic ceremonial and administrative centre in the heart of modern-day Lima.

The body was found inside an underground ceremonial canal, lying on its left side with its skull tilted westward towards the sea and a mud pyramid within the complex.

Archaeologist Gladys Paz, who is leading the excavation, says the position of the remains points to an intentional ritual placement.

"We are looking at the discovery of a human offering found inside a ceremonial canal belonging to the Lima culture," said Paz. "We are located at Huaca Pucllana, which corresponds to Sector B of Huaca Chica, at what would have been the main gate or entrance to the ceremonial center around 650 AD."

An archaeologist holds up a ceramic snake head that he unearthed while excavating skeletal remains at the Huaca Pucllana archaeological site in Lima, Peru. Martin Mejia - AP

The discovery offers archaeologists an opportunity to learn more about how ceremonies were conducted at the site more than 1,300 years ago.

The excavation has also uncovered ceramic pieces, adding further evidence of activity at the ceremonial centre.

Huaca Pucllana is part of the modern landscape of Lima, where ancient archaeological sites can be found alongside the city's homes, businesses and public infrastructure.

Archaeologist Micaela Alvarez says this contrast is one of the features that makes the site particularly striking for visitors.

"It's a characteristic of Huaca Pucllana for quite a few decades now; in fact, it’s almost what attracts people who come to visit us, to find such an ancient archaeological site right in the middle of the city; it’s surprising, really."

Skeletal remains are exposed while being excavated by archeologists at the Huaca Pucllana archaeological site in Lima, Peru, Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. Martin Mejia - AP

The Lima culture flourished on Peru's central coast between 100 and 700 AD, before the rise of the Inca Empire.

Pucllana was one of its major ceremonial and administrative centres.

The discovery is not an isolated example of Lima's pre-Hispanic past. More than 400 sacred sites belonging to pre-Hispanic cultures are scattered throughout the capital, according to official data.

The remains are expected to be removed from the excavation site in the coming days.

For archaeologists, the find provides another glimpse into the rituals and beliefs of the people who lived in the area long before modern Lima was founded.

World.title: Champagne harvest: why picking begins as early as mid-August
World.content:
In Champagne, the calendar seems to have gone into overdrive. On the hillsides of Hautvillers, grape-pickers are already hard at work even though August is not yet over. This year, the first picking officially started between 12 and 17 August, depending on the area and the grape variety. An exceptionally early start that speaks volumes about how the climate is changing in the region.

 

For Alexandre Gobillard, production director at the Gobillard & Fils house, harvesting this early was once unthinkable.

"I've been working on the estate for 30 years, and when I started my father always used to say: 'On 15 August, go on holiday.' Today it's 18 August and we're in the middle of the harvest. We've never seen anything like it." he explains.

The heat has dramatically sped up the ripening of the grapes. After a spell of frost at the end of March (another first), Champagne then endured several heatwaves and severe drought. Temperatures even reached 40°C in June in some parts of the region.

The drought has also increased the concentration of sugars in the grapes. Winegrowers therefore have to monitor ripeness extremely closely to strike the right balance and produce champagne that is sufficiently fresh and delicate.

A little further east, in Tours-sur-Marne, the situation is the same. The owner of these vines, Ophélie Lapie-Lamiable, can only observe that for the past twenty years or so, especially since the 2003 heatwave, the harvest has systematically been brought forward and that people will probably have to get used to it.

"2003 is still remembered as a landmark year. It was the first time we harvested at the end of August in Champagne. Since 2003, we've already harvested at the end of August at least ten times, and so 2026 will probably also go down in history for its frost and its earliness. Perhaps in 20 years' time we'll be saying that in the end, harvesting on 15 August has more or less become normal." says Ophélie Lapie-Lamiable, manager of Champagne Lamiable.

Champagne served in a glass. AP Photo

Adapting to global warming at all costs

This shift is already forcing the industry to rethink its practices and to look at grape varieties that can better withstand climate change. It also makes organising the harvest more complicated, as it is traditionally carried out by hand, with thousands of seasonal workers who need to be housed and transported in the height of summer, sometimes in sweltering heat.

Out in the vineyards, the first signs are still encouraging. The question now is what this lightning-quick harvest will produce once the wine is in the bottle.

In the cellars, the grapes are already being pressed. The first bubbles of this very early vintage are therefore beginning to take shape, and it will take a few years to know whether they have also lived up to all their promise and are considered a grand cru.

World.title: ICC separates Taliban probe from US case as Afghan women's fate stays uncertain
World.content:
Five years after Afghanistan fell into the hands of the Taliban as they captured Kabul, the International Criminal Court has reportedly split its investigation of Taliban crimes from the broader Afghanistan probe in a move that could ease pressure from Washington on the court.

 

According to Middle East Eye, judges at the ICC's Pre-Trial Chamber II have ordered prosecutors to open a standalone investigation into alleged Taliban persecution of women, separating it from the court's long-running Afghanistan investigation, which also covered alleged crimes by US personnel.

The Chamber reportedly found that Taliban conduct since 2021 is "materially different" from the conduct the original investigation was authorised to examine, and directed prosecutors to open a standalone inquiry.

The ICC's Office of the Prosecutor would neither confirm nor deny the decision to Euronews, but it did indicate that the Taliban are the core concern of its probe.

“The investigation is focused on the Taliban leadership and their alleged crimes of persecuting women and political opponents, including the deprivation of fundamental rights, systematic arrests and torture,” a spokesperson said.

"The Office of the Prosecutor is unable to provide further comment on the investigation, or on the existence or non-existence of any alleged Court filing which is not public," the spokesperson added.

‘Deeply troubling’

Shaharzad Akbar, former head of the Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission and now a fellow at Oxford's Wolfson College, did not mince words on the split.

"Any selective justice is deeply troubling," Akbar told Euronews. "It is also alarming to hear the US's bullying, intimidation and attacks on the court are influencing decisions made about investigations."

Akbar said Afghan civil society groups have "repeatedly asked the ICC for comprehensive investigations about all allegations that fall within its mandate," including allegations against US forces, and described Washington's conduct toward the court throughout the investigation as "appalling and shameful”.

FILE: US Special Forces soldier takes cover as two Chinook Ch-47 helicopters come in for a landing with supplies in Afghanistan, 16 September 2009 AP Photo

The allegations against US personnel in Afghanistan relate primarily to the documented abuse of detainees at CIA detention facilities there, including the Salt Pit black site north of Kabul, and the conduct of US military interrogators.

The US Senate Intelligence Committee's 2014 report on the CIA's detention and interrogation programme found that detainees were subjected to waterboarding, sleep deprivation and other methods that constitute degradation and torture.

The next day, the US Justice Department announced it would not open any new criminal investigations as a result of its findings. It also stated that if any foreign government issued an arrest warrant for a US official in connection with the programme, it would not enforce it.

No US government has ever acknowledged wrongdoing by US military or CIA personnel in Afghanistan.

During US President Donald Trump's first term, the White House applauded an early ICC ruling that declined to open a formal investigation into US personnel’s actions in Afghanistan, calling it "a major international victory" for "patriots”. The decision was later repealed.

Why were the two bundled together to begin with?

Unlike other international tribunals, the ICC does not separate its investigations by belligerents in a conflict. It probes what it calls a "situation” defined by territory and time period.

Afghanistan ratified the Rome Statute in 2003, giving the court jurisdiction over crimes committed on Afghan soil from that date, regardless of who committed them.

When the Appeals Chamber authorised a formal investigation in 2020, it covered the Taliban and its affiliate the Haqqani network, the so-called Islamic State-Khorasan Province group (ISIS-K), Afghan government forces, and US military and CIA personnel, all under a single investigative umbrella.

FILE: The International Criminal Court, or ICC, is seen in The Hague, 7 November 2019 AP Photo

In 2021, then-prosecutor Karim Khan deprioritised the part of the investigation concerning US conduct, choosing to focus the court’s resources on the Taliban and ISIS-K.

But because the broader Afghanistan “situation” remained formally open, long-standing political pressure from Washington aimed at the investigation as a whole had the potential to affect the case against the Taliban simply because both were part of the same file.

That pressure became even more pronounced ever since Trump returned to office in January 2025, with his administration doling out further sanctions within months against ICC officials tied to the Afghanistan and Palestine investigations.

In December, diplomats told Middle East Eye that at the court's oversight meeting, Washington pressed for both investigations to be dropped entirely as a condition for lifting sanctions on ICC officials.

The July 2025 warrants against Taliban leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and judiciary chief Abdul Hakim Haqqani for the crime against humanity of persecution of women and those perceived as allies of women on political grounds were issued amid those pressures.

Washington to bring down the court?

Last month, the US State Department announced plans for a campaign to “dismantle” the court and "systematically disable" its "ability to operate (and to) target American servicemen or officials, or otherwise threaten American sovereignty."

It said actions could include increased restrictions and visa revocations, as well as travel bans on ICC personnel.

On Tuesday, Washington announced further sanctions on ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye, accusing them of "directly" engaging "in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction."

FILE: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio listens as President Donald Trump speaks during a roundtable at the State Department in Washington, 7 August 2026 AP Photo

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who called the ICC a "corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court," added that it had "maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate.”

The court "repeatedly attempted to assert authority over nationals of the United States and other countries that have not consented to its jurisdiction or ratified the Rome Statute,” according to Rubio.

The US has never ratified the Rome Statute. President Bill Clinton signed it in his final days in office in December 2000, but the administration of George W Bush formally withdrew the signature in May 2002 and notified the UN that the US did not intend to become a party.

US Congress followed that same year with the American Service Members' Protection Act, which authorises the president to use military force to free any US citizen or allied national held by the ICC, legislation informally dubbed the "Hague Invasion Act”.

‘A gift to the Taliban’

Meanwhile, Washington’s actions after pulling out of Afghanistan have gone beyond abandonment, according to Akbar.

"This context has emboldened criminal conduct and extensive violations across the world," she said. "This is a gift to regimes like the Taliban, who can continue with impunity in a context of failing global order and rule of law."

“US’ disregard for international law and its attacks on the court embolden actors like Taliban and feed into their narratives about the Western bias of international tribunals."

Afghanistan under the Taliban has turned into the most repressive country in the world for women, according to a UN assessment in March 2024.

FILE: An Afghan woman takes part in a rally to mark International Women's Day, in Islamabad, Pakistan, 8 March 2023 AP Photo

Since August 2021, the Taliban have issued more than 50 decrees systematically removing women from public life in Afghanistan.

Girls are banned from education beyond the sixth grade, making Afghanistan the only country in the world where women are barred from secondary school on the basis of their gender.

Women are prohibited from working in most jobs, including working for NGOs and UN agencies. Parks, gyms and public spaces are also off-limits.

Further edicts were issued with the intent to persecute LGBTQ+ Afghans, empowering "morality police" to punish "moral crimes" and explicitly criminalising same-sex intimacy.

Akbar said that Afghan women's rights groups, human rights investigators and survivors "have supported the ICC investigation every step of the way and have contributed to the process," while also demanding that the court widens its scope.

What happens now?

None of the Taliban officials under warrant are likely to ever be in custody: the group has complete control over Afghan territory since the US withdrawal in 2021 and has dismissed warrants as “hostility towards Islam”.

Akhundzada has led the Taliban since 2016, when he succeeded Mullah Akhtar Mansour after his death in a US drone strike in Pakistan. Akhundzada has never appeared in public since taking on the role and is believed to operate solely from Kandahar in southern Afghanistan.

He is ultimately responsible for the most restrictive edicts against women.

Chief justice Haqqani has been the main architect of the judicial tools enforcing those edicts, including the return of public floggings and executions.

Asked what the warrants have achieved, Akbar said that although valuable, they have had limited impact.

"We welcomed the news of arrest warrants because it was a moment of justice and accountability after decades of impunity in Afghanistan," she said. "We hoped the warrants would also delay the trend of normalisation of the Taliban."

"To change the situation in Afghanistan we need stronger political will from the region and the Western countries to engage on similar terms with the Taliban and demand reversals on bans and restrictions on the rights and freedoms of women and girls in Afghanistan,” Akbar concluded.

World.title: South Africa's ANC faces voter backlash
World.content:
Anti-migrant violence, economic stagnation and corruption allegations are eroding support for South Africa's ruling ANC ahead of local elections in November, opening the door to new coalition possibilities.

Impassable roads, crater-like potholes, burst water pipes, mountains of trash, and grinding poverty are part of everyday life in South Africa's communities. So too are unemployment, hunger, and crime.

The latest wave of violence targeting foreign nationals has claimed several lives since April and forced more than 176,000 people to flee South Africa, most of them returning to their home countries of neighboring Zimbabwe, Malawi and Mozambique.

Anti-foreigner anger escalates

At the recently concluded Southern African Development Community (SADC) summit in Durban, the vigilante group March and March again called for migrants to leave South Africa.

"Come and take your people back," its members urged the governments of neighboring countries, while police moved to contain the protests.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said ahead of the summit that he was "concerned and ashamed" that citizens of other countries had been subjected to abuse and violence and had been forced to flee.

According to Fredson Guilengue of the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, growing anti-migrant sentiment is a symptom of deeper public discontent.

"This reflects their frustration, particularly with the ANC's failure at both the national and local levels to create jobs, tackle inequality, reduce crime and improve living conditions," Guilengue told DW. "In the [November 4] elections, South Africans will express their deep frustration over the lack of public services, inadequate infrastructure and poverty."

ANC support continues to erode

The African National Congress (ANC), Nelson Mandela's former liberation party, is on course to perform even worse than in the 2024 general election, when it suffered a historic setback, winning 40.2% of the vote, Guilengue notes.

South Africa's municipal elections will gauge public sentiment on the government of national unity (GNU) under Ramaphosa Image: Jerome Delay/AP Photo/picture alliance

According to Guilengue, the November elections are unlikely to go in the ANC's favor, as little has changed for the better since the last election. In other words, unemployment remains very high, as do crime rates and corruption.

"These problems have not been resolved over the years and have become entrenched in South African society. The municipalities have been governed by the ANC, and there has been widespread mismanagement alongside a steady deterioration of infrastructure. That has generated enormous public anger," he added.

Voters are expected to turn to opposition parties, including the main opposition Democratic Alliance (DA), a party supported primarily by white voters and one that has been part of a government of national unity with the ANC since 2024.

In a surprise move, former Cape Town mayor Helen Zille, known as the "Iron Lady," is running as the DA's mayoral candidate in Johannesburg in the upcoming local elections, hoping to rescue the country's economic hub from its deep crisis.

"She will run a very strong campaign, which could benefit the DA and hurt the ANC," Guilengue said.

Political analysts say the ANC has faced persistent leadership challenges in recent years, and they have noted that, although impeachment proceedings against President Cyril Ramaphosahave been suspended for the time being, they have damaged his public image.

Dirty money in the president's sofa?

Ramaphosa came under suspicion of money laundering in 2020 after half a million US dollars was stolen from a sofa on his Phala Phala game farm. He has always denied wrongdoing and ​said the $580,000 ‌stolen was proceeds from the sale of buffaloes.

"The ANC's strategy is to drag out these proceedings so that they do not coincide with this year's elections, at least," Guilengue said. "Possibly until the next general election in 2029, when Ramaphosa will no longer be eligible to serve as president because his second term will then have ended in accordance with the constitution."

South Africa sees nationwide protests over migrants To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ANC leadership, which is supposed to be fighting corruption, is itself facing allegations of corruption, noted Guilengue.

Analyst Daniel Silke speaks of a further "erosion of the ANC," saying it will become increasingly difficult for the party to retain its grip on power at the national level as its approval ratings continue to decline.

"We are witnessing a continuing turning point in South African politics that began in 2024: the gradual disintegration of the former liberation movement. The black electorate is more polarized and fragmented than ever, and among former ANC supporters, the shine has come off the liberation movement," Silke told DW.

He identifies three key characteristics of present-day South Africa:a stagnant economy, a shrinking manufacturing sector, and a lack of trust in political and security institutions as well as in the country's governance. "That's an almost perfect recipe for discontent.”

According to Silke, the key question in this election is whether former ANC voters will turn out and vote for opposition parties or stay away from the polls altogether.

Coalition deals hold the key

Silke said that South Africans will likely spread their votes around, not only to the DA but also to the MK Party (uMkhonto weSizwe) of former president Jacob Zuma, and to ethnically aligned minority parties such as the Patriotic Alliance and the Freedom Front Plus, as well as ActionSA.

The analyst added that smaller political parties, alongside the main opposition Democratic Alliance (DA), will create more opportunities for coalition governments.

"Governance will be challenging, as complex coalitions, potentially including the ANC, will need to be stabilized in order to provide South Africa with at least the semblance of effective public service delivery," Silke told DW.

He added that the best South Africans can hope for is a multiparty arrangement that brings moderate forces together rather than populist ones.

However, according to Silke, the ANC and the DA remain by far the country's two largest parties, even though neither is anywhere close to securing 50% of the vote. "How they choose their coalition partners will determine South Africa's future."

Thousands leave S. Africa over threats of xenophobic attacks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: How DW fact-checks fake news
World.content:
Disinformation spreads fast. Step inside DW's fact-checking process and see how the team puts online claims to the test.

Not sure who to trust or where to find reliable, fact-based information?

False and misleading claims can spread around the world in a matter of minutes, making it increasingly difficult to separate fact from fiction.

At a time when false claims can spread faster than facts, independent verification is essential.

That's where DW Fact check comes in. Allow us to introduce ourselves and explain more about our work.

How DW's fact-checking team works To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What topics we choose

DW fact-checkers investigate a wide range of claims and stories.

This can include statements made by politicians, government officials and political parties, as well as claims involving celebrities, athletes, business leaders and non-profit organizations.

We verify the authenticity of images, videos or audios that go viral on major social media platforms.

Increasingly, we also investigate whether widely shared content is authentic or has been generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence.

To decide which topics to fact-check, we assess claims based on four criteria:

Virality: How quickly is a narrative spreading? Reach: Is the narrative being shared across multiple platforms and/or in multiple languages? Relevance: Why does the topic matter to our target audience? How important is it to the public debate? Impact: What consequences could the spread of the narrative have?

How we verify information

DW has created a dedicated website where you can learn more about the verification workflows and tools we regularly use. Image: DW

At DW Fact check, we investigate the origin of a claim, when and where it emerged, whether it has been manipulated, and who is behind it.

Whenever possible, we trace claims back to their original source and examine the evidence supporting them. We then compare the claim with reliable data, documents and expert assessments to determine its accuracy.

To fact-check information, we use a range of open-source intelligence (OSINT) tools and verification techniques.

DW has created a dedicated website where you can learn more about the verification workflows and tools we regularly use. There, you can explore methods for verifying images, videos, audio recordings, sources and text-based claims.

Transparency is an essential part of our work. Every fact check includes hyperlinks to the sources used in our reporting whenever possible, allowing readers to review the same evidence our journalists relied on.

Like all DW journalism, our fact checks are based on information that has been verified through reliable and independent sources.

Whenever possible, we follow the two-source principle and seek confirmation from more than one source.

While sourcing information from interview partners, we always select reliable and unbiased people. All interviews are recorded, with the consent of the interview partner, and archived.

We mention all sources by name and occupation and, where possible, link to their contact information so there is no lack of transparency.

Anonymity is only granted to sources in rare cases when their security is at stake or the topic is sensitive. In these cases, we are transparent about the reasons for granting anonymity.

How we rate claims

From the World Cup to elections and conflicts, major events are often accompanied by a flood of false and misleading claims.

DW uses a collaborative process to evaluate claims and determine verdicts.

Before publication, the lead reporter recommends a verdict to two editors.

The rating system has eight categories:

True: The statement is accurate.

The statement is accurate. False: The statement is not accurate.

The statement is not accurate. Misleading: The statement is partially correct, but the information is portrayed in a way that creates a wrong impression.

The statement is partially correct, but the information is portrayed in a way that creates a wrong impression. Unproven: The statement cannot be proven true or false.

The statement cannot be proven true or false. Fake: The image, video or audio is manipulated.

The image, video or audio is manipulated. Real: The image, video or audio is authentic.

The image, video or audio is authentic. AI- generated: The image, video or audio was created using artificial intelligence.

The image, video or audio was created using artificial intelligence. AI- manipulated: The image, video or audio was altered using artificial intelligence.

How we use artificial intelligence

At DW Fact check we clearly label any content that we verify as having been generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence. Image: Instagram

DW has clear editorial guidelines when it comes to the use of artificial intelligence in journalism.

AI can help us improve workflows, accessibility, translation, data and content analysis and format adaptation. However, humans remain responsible for every journalistic decision and every item we publish.

You can read DW’s ten AI editorial guidelines here.

At DW Fact check we clearly label any content that we verify as having been generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence. We also explicitly disclose when we have used AI tools to help us verify content.

As part of our verification workflow we may use AI detectors to help assess whether content has been created or manipulated with AI. But because these detectors often produce inaccurate results, we use them with great caution. We use multiple tools to reduce the risk of error.

AI detectors do not determine our conclusions on their own. Any findings are reviewed and verified by our journalists using additional evidence.

Fact-checking isn't just about exposing fakes. It's also about confirming what's real. Here, DW verified that a viral video showing destruction in Gaza was authentic. Image: Instagram/m_abu.samra/palestine.pixel

How we correct mistakes

We do not manipulate images or videos we broadcast. When we correct or revise a text, or blur or zoom in on a video, we indicate which changes have been made and why.

We are committed to providing accurate and high-quality content free of errors.

However, despite numerous quality control measures, mistakes can happen.

At DW, it is important that we address these errors as soon as we become aware of them, and do so transparently. This means that when we publish an item that needs to be revised, we need to clearly indicate any changes that have been made.

This also applies to mistakes involving numbers, dates, names, locations, quotes and photos. These are corrected as soon as they have been verified, and the item is republished for online and social media.

A note added to the bottom of the article (or in a social media thread) informs the user of the revision and reason.

You can read DW's full guidelines on dealing with errors here.

How we work with other fact-checking organizations

The International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) is an association of fact-checkers worldwide, with more than one hundred organizations as members.

DW Fact check has been a member since March 2024. Membership must be confirmed annually with an application process.

To be accepted into the network, members must prove that they guarantee a high level of credibility based on 31 criteria.

With the "Code of Principles," members commit themselves to non-partisanship and open and honest corrections, among other criteria.

If you believe that DW Fact check violates the IFCN Code of Principles, you can contact the IFCN here and file a complaint.

Moreover, DW is part of the ARD Fact-Check Network, which combines the expertise of fact-checking teams from across Germany’s ARD public broadcasters.

Impartiality rules at DW

Like all DW journalism, our fact checks are based on information that has been verified through reliable and independent sources. Image: Horst Galuschka/dpa/picture alliance

At DW, we are committed to impartiality. Across our coverage, and especially when reporting on controversial topics, we strive to include diverse voices and divergent views.

As individuals with our own lived experiences, we each have personal views and opinions — but these are private views that should not have an effect on our coverage.

We strive to always stick to these impartiality rules and maintain the highest standards of ethical journalism. They are based on the "Basic principles of the programs" as defined in §5 of the Deutsche Welle Act.

To sum it up, our fact checks rely on in-depth research using OSINT tools, independent sources, transparency, detailed argumentation, clear verdicts and DW's standards of impartial and unbiased journalism.

How you can reach the team

DW also encourages readers and viewers to submit suggestions and claims they have encountered.

We regularly review and report on these topics. We also encourage users to leave comments on our social media posts or write to us directly with questions or concerns.

While we review every message we receive wherever possible, we cannot guarantee that we will investigate every claim. Whether we pursue a topic depends on our editorial criteria, our resources and our ability to verify a claim.

You can reach us at factchecking@dw.com. Don’t hesitate to get in touch.

This article was first published in 2023 and has been revised to incorporate new developments and trends. Rachel Baig contributed to the original report. Edited by Josh Axelrod.

World.title: How to better protect Europe from wildfires
World.content:
In another summer of European wildfires that have even seen wetlands burning, scientists say the situation is set to worsen in the future. What's needed is fire prevention and climate protection.

From Spain and France to Portugal, Greece and Italy, the list of European countries affected by particularly severe wildfires is long. It even includes colder states such as the UK, Ireland and Norway.

This summer, extreme heat and prolonged drought have heightened the risk of wildfires, which have destroyed more than 6,000 square kilometers of forest and forced hundreds of thousands to leave their homes. By early August, the damage carried an estimated price tag of €15 billion ($17.5 billion).

And according to a study published today by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK), the coming decades are likely to see the wildfire risk in Europe worsen.

Annual burned area could triple

The researchers found that even with significantly stronger climate action, 39% more land could be burning annually by the end of the century than it is today.

"If we continue to produce more emissions and global temperatures rise by around 3.6 degrees Celsius (6.48 Fahrenheit), wildfires will become much more frequent, especially in the Mediterranean region and across large parts of western and central Europe, including areas that have experienced few fires so far," said PIK researcher Maik Billing, lead author of the study published in the scientific journal Global Change Biology.

The international community originally agreed to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, or at least to well below 2C. However, countries are still falling far short on their climate targets.

At the same time, the effects of global warming are becoming increasingly visible. According to the study, by early August, twice as much land had already burned in Europe during this summer's heatwave season than in recent years.

Fire prevention could save seven times its costs

Yet Thomas Hickler, a researcher at the Senckenberg Society for Nature Research, which contributed to the study, says Europe is not powerless in the face of this growing threat.

"We see fire-conducive conditions increasing, so we need to invest more," he said.

Wildfire management, improved training and equipment for emergency responders, as well as stronger coordination between forestry authorities, conservation bodies and fire services can "make a substantial difference," according to Hickler.

The Netherlands has also been affected by wildfires this summer Image: Arnulf Stoffel/Funke Foto Services/IMAGO

The European Union's contribution to forest and wildfire management programs in member states between 2021 and 2027 is around €2.1 billion. And according to World Bank estimates, such investments can pay off — with every euro spent on prevention saving up to seven euros on firefighting and reconstruction.

The role of polluting emissions

If the greenhouse gas emissions generated by burning fossil fuels to power our homes and industries were to fall rapidly and sharply limit global warming, effective fire management could reduce future burned areas by as much as 90%.

However, the study argues that significantly stronger climate action will still be necessary if wildfires are to remain under control in the long term.

"Climate change could create conditions so extreme that we reach the limits of what is still feasible in preventing and fighting fires once they grow beyond a certain size," said Kirsten Thonicke of PIK, a co-author of the study.

Meanwhile wildfires have been burning for days in western Germany and neighboring Belgium.

In the High Fens, a cross-border forest and wetland region connecting the two countries, around 3,000 hectares of vegetation have been scorched in recent days. It is the largest wildfire Belgium has seen in decades.

Why wetlands burn too

Wetlands such as marshes and raised bogs may seem safe from fire. But when they dry out during droughts, as is currently happening in the High Fens, their peat soil, which is formed from an accumulation of dead plant material, makes them vulnerable to fire .

For centuries, peat was used as fuel for heating and cooking. But it's also highly polluting. When layers of peat several meters thick burn, carbon that has been stored in the soil for thousands of years can be released in a very short time.

Although wetlands cover only about 3% of the Earth's surface, they store around 30% of the carbon contained in soils worldwide.

Wetlands become highly flammable if they dry out, either as a result of drought or human intervention Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

While conventional forest fires are often characterized by high flames, peat ones smoulder underground. They burn at relatively low temperatures, produce large amounts of smoke but often have barely visible flames. And they are extremely difficult to extinguish, sometimes persisting for months and even continuing to burn through the winter.

They also release large quantities of pollutants, including smoke particles and hazardous heavy metals such as mercury.

Massive peat fires in Canada and Siberia in recent years have demonstrated the scale such fires can reach. A peat fire in Indonesia in 1997, which affected roughly 100,000 square kilometres, ranks among the largest environmental disasters of the 20th century.

In a study published in Nature, scientists estimated that this single fire may have released between 13 and 40% of total global emissions in 1997.

Across Indonesia and neighboring countries, more than 200,000 people were treated in hospitals for acute health problems. As a direct consequence of this and other major fires, several Southeast Asian nations adopted an agreement aimed at combating transboundary air pollution a few years later.

For Europe, the new study delivers a clear message: if global temperatures continue to rise as scientists predict, improved wildfire management may help limit the danger but will not be enough to eliminate it.



This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Ukraine: Several killed in 'massive' Russian strikes on Kyiv
World.content:
The strikes on the Ukrainian capital and its surrounding regions also injured dozens, damaged buildings and caused power cuts. In neighboring Poland, the military started preventive operations to protect its airspace.

Overnight Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, and its surrounding regions killed at least 13 people and injured more than 30, Ukrainian authorities said early Thursday.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said that Moscow had launched a massive ballistic missile attack on the city and that cleanup operations were still underway. He called for Friday to be observed as a day of mourning.

What do we know about the Russian attacks?

The attacks damaged residential buildings, a medical facility and an educational institution, the Kyiv city military administration said in a statement. The power supply in some parts of the capital was also cut.

At least 13 people were killed in Kyiv, officials said.

Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent months Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

Klitschko said seven people died in the city's Solomianskyi district, where a fire broke out and the upper floors of a nine-story residential block were destroyed.

Which other areas were hit?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia also attacked gas infrastructure in the northern Chernihiv region and a border crossing with Moldova in the southern Odesa region.

"It was ‌a massive ‌attack — the ​Russians had been preparing for a long ​time, combining different types of ⁠ballistic missiles, ​cruise ​missiles, and drones, ​aiming to ‌cause as much damage ​as ⁠possible to civilian infrastructure," ⁠Zelenskyy ​said on social media.

Ukraine has a critical shortage of interceptors to down ballistic missiles, a weakness Russia has sought to exploit.

The Russian Defense Ministry said it had targeted facilities producing drone components, a military depot and a logistics hub in the attacks on Kyiv and its surrounds.

Ukraine faces Patriot missile shortage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In neighboring Poland, the Polish army said it started preventive military aviation operations to protect its airspace amid the Russian strikes. The Polish military often takes this measure amid heavy Russian strikes on Ukraine.

In Romania, the Defense Ministry said a drone crashed into an uninhabited area of the country of Tulcea during the Russian attacks. The ministry added that radar systems detected aerial targets near the Ukrainian border, prompting the scrambling of two Spanish fighter jets deployed on NATO missions and a Romanian air force helicopter.

A drone also crossed Moldova's airspace, the country's military said.

Escalation on both sides

Russia has stepped up attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent months, with Ukraine also increasing attacks deep within Russia.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 250 drones had flown toward the Moscow region between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.

Diplomatic efforts have failed to reach a ceasefire in the war, which started with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

World.title: Bernadette Amani 'living her dream' at Bayern Munich
World.content:
Bernadette Amani is heading into her first full season with Bayern Munich, having joined the club in January. Making a living at football is something she never imagined possible while growing up in rural Ivory Coast.

Several months after moving to Germany, Bernadette Amani is clearly where she wants to be, having won both the Bundesliga and the German Cup in her first half-season since joining Bayern Munich.

"It's a dream come true for me to be here, and I'm living my dream to the full," the 28-year-old midfielder told DW in a recent exclusive interview.

"Munich is a very, very big club. Beyond just making me happy, it's a real achievement, a dream come true to be here, to play for such a prestigious club."

Amani, who recently captained Ivory Coast at the Women's Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON), added that playing for Bayern's women has been a major step up from what she had come to know playing for CD Tenerife Femenino of Liga F, Spain's topflight.

"I was already professional when I was in Spain, but let's just say it wasn't quite the same level of professionalism," she explained.

"In Spain or the Ivory Coast, the coaching staff might have consisted of no more than five or six people. But here there are eight or 10 people. And that enables them (the players) to perform at that high level for a long time."

This structure, and the experience of the players around her, she said, make it virtually impossible for a new player not to improve on their own game.

"I've learned a great deal about aspects I wasn't already aware of; how to position myself, how to position my body, how to interact with the ball and how to think. Really understanding the game is something I'm gradually learning alongside (the players) and the coaching staff."

At Bayern for less than a year Bernadette Amani says the professional environment has helped make her a better player Image: Jenni Maul/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

Moving to the capital to further education

Getting to the Bundesliga champions was anything but a straight, plotted path for Amani, who, when she began kicking a ball with the boys in her local village as a youngster, had no idea that football could be a career option.

Her parents were anything but encouraging of her passion. They just wanted their daughter to get a good education. To this end, she wound up moving from the village of Dougbafla, where she grew up, to the capital, Abidjan — a move that turned out to be pivotal to her career as a footballer.

"I discovered the women's football league. I went to a match and, as luck would have it, it was the top team against the second-placed team," she recalled.

"I saw the intensity, I saw the technique, and then I heard that so-and-so isn't here today because she's playing in Serbia, another isn't here today because she's playing in Turkey. And that was a real eye-opener for me; it made me realize that I could make a living from what I love."

Bayern's 4-0 win over Wolfsburg in the final gave Bernadette Amani her second title in Munich Image: Nico Herbertz/IMAGO

One of the clubs she watched on that day in 2019, Onze Soeurs de Gagnoa, offered her a trial – and she made the team. Within a year, she was in Spain's third tier, and five years later, she found herself in Liga F with Eibar. Always looking to take that next step, she quickly moved on to Tenerife, her launching pad for Bayern, which she describes as "the top." Still, there's no question of complacency.

"Someone on the outside will say to you: 'You've put in the effort, you've made it to Bayern, a club that wins titles, that's professional and renowned all over the world," she said.

"But someone who's involved in football will tell you that's where the hard part begins. Staying there is even better. And it's hard not to let your guard down."

Disappointment at WAFCON

With Bayern about to start their Women's Bundesliga title defense against Union Berlin, Amani is back in the Bavarian capital following what will have been a disappointing Women's Africa Cup of Nations for the Ivory Coast. Prior to the tournament, Amani had told DW that her team's goal would be "to do no worse than we did at the last Africa Cup of Nations we took part in — that is, to finish third."

However, not only did Ivory Coast fall to Algeria 2-1 in the quarterfinals, but to make matters worse, they've failed to qualify for next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil. Ivory Coast fell 2-1 to Ghana in one of two play-in matches for the inter-confederation playoffs, the last possible path to the World Cup.

While male players tend to get time off after a major summer tournament, Amani was already back on the Bayern bench for Saturday's DFB Supercup win over Wolfsburg (3-0) – just two days after Ivory Coast's defeat to Ghana in Casablanca. Now the focus is squarely back on retaining Bayern's Women's Bundesliga title.

Ali Farhat contributed to this article.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

World.title: North Korea fires possible ballistic missiles toward sea
World.content:
The launch came hours after US President Trump announced plans to meet Kim Jong Un later this year.

North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea on Thursday, South Korea's military said.

Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said the North fired the missiles "from its Pyongyang area."

Earlier, the Japanese prime minister's office and the country's Coast Guard also said they detected the suspected launch.

The incident came hours after US President Donald Trump said he would meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un later this year.

US-South Korea military drills shortened

The latest missile launches also come as South Korea and the US continue military drills that are set to end Friday after Trump's order to significantly reduce US participation.

Pyongyang has long denounced US-South Korea joint exercises as invasion rehearsals, often responding with missile launches.

Trump described the war games as "inappropriate and hostile," on Wednesday as he announced he would meet Kim later this year,

"These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful," he wrote on Truth Social.

Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of Kim Jong Un, dismissed Trump’s move, saying, "The provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won't change even though their duration and size were reduced."

"If the US calculates that it can propagate its recent measure as the one of so-called good faith, they will not get the desired answer," she added.

Police in Pune in the western state of Maharashtra have registered a case against eight people from a right-wing group accused of assaulting domestic tourists after taking offense at an 8-year-old girl wearing shorts.

The incident occurred at the city's Sinhagad Fort on Sunday, a day after India's Independence Day.
