World.title: Mikee Romero retires from AFP Reserve Force amid medals controversy
World.content:
The former congressman also relinquishes his post as wing commander of the Tactical Operations Wing Reserve Northern Luzon 'effective immediately'

MANILA, Philippines – Businessman and former 1-Pacman congressman Michael “Mikee” Romero has retired from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Reserve Force, amid questions raised over his military awards.

“With gratitude and respect, I hereby formally relinquish all my duties and responsibilities as Wing Commander of the Tactical Operations Wing Reserve Northern Luzon and retire from the Reserve Force of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), effective immediately,” Romero said in a letter addressed to AFP chief General Antonio Nafarrete dated August 19.

Romero, who held the rank of brigadier general in the Philippine Air Force (PAF) Reserve, made the move days after his photo with Nafarrete made the rounds on social media. The photo showed the former congressman in uniform with seemingly more medals than the AFP chief himself, raising questions about how Romero, a reserve officer, got so many medals in the first place.

Among the medals allegedly spotted on Romero was the Gold Cross Medal, which is the fourth highest military award given to personnel for acts of gallantry. Romero denied this and said his Gawad sa Kapayapaan medal — for helping the AFP acquire three new C-130 aircraft when he was still a congressman — was mistaken for the Gold Cross Medal.

An example of a Gold Cross Medal recipient is Scout Ranger Captain Gromel Auman, who was killed in action during a firefight with Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters (BIFF) on March 8, 2015.

On Wednesday, August 19, the AFP said in a statement that it was “reviewing its policies and procedures on the recruitment, promotion, and conferment of awards to personnel of the Reserve Force.”

The AFP said it “remains committed to upholding the integrity, meritocracy, and credibility of its processes. Any verified irregularities shall be addressed in accordance with existing rules and regulations.”

“The AFP recognizes the valuable contributions of its reservists and will continue to ensure that the standards governing the Reserve Force are properly observed,” it added.

The AFP also cited an ongoing PAF investigation into the matter.

The PAF said the investigation will address concerns regarding the promotions and decorations to reserve personnel. It said this will include a review “of the affected personnel records, orders, and promotion boards.”

“Any verified irregularities or policy violations resulting from this investigation will be dealt with decisively under existing rules and regulations to preserve the credibility and standards of the Air Force Reserve Service,” the PAF said.

Among those who backed the review was Senate Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, a Philippine Military Academy graduate who had served in the Philippine Constabulary and the Philippine National Police.

“Behind every ribbon pinned on a soldier’s uniform represents a medal. Every medal has a unique story about heroism, valor, courage and bravery, or an outstanding feat even outside the combat zone,” Lacson said in a social media post on Wednesday. – Rappler.com

World.title: PNP: 74 cases linked to nihilistic violent extremism, 42 minors rescued so far
World.content:
PNP-ACG. Colonel Richmond Tadina of the Anti-Cybercrime Group of the PNP discusses the NVE cases in the Philippines at a Senate hearing, on August 20.

Senator Risa Hontiveros calls for urgent action and accountability from social media platforms amid the rise in NVE cases

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group (PNP-ACG) has handled 74 cases linked to nihilistic violent extremism (NVE) and rescued 42 minors in connection with these cases, officials told a Senate hearing on Thursday, August 20.

The figure visibly shocked Senator Risa Hontiveros, who is leading the Senate inquiry into the Zamboanga school shooting and the broader threat of NVE.

“This is terrible proof that this is a real problem,” Hontiveros said after hearing the number as she called for a more proactive, coordinated response to prevent NVE from becoming a pattern in the Philippines.

Of the 42 minors rescued, 30 were aged 15 and younger, with many falling within the 12-to-15 age range, according to Police Colonel Richmond Tadina of the PNP-ACG. Their leads for these cases come from schools and parents, as well as referrals connected to Meta and the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

Tadina said the cases are a geographically “borderless” problem. The PNP-ACG has not seen or identified any local groomers.

CICC Executive Director Aboy Paraiso noted the concern on how foreign extremist ideas can influence young Filipinos.

“What we are trying to prevent here in the Philippines [are] the copycats and the influence of NVE,” Paraiso told the hearing.

He said the ideology associated with NVE groups are mostly foreign to the Philippines, citing racism and white supremacy as examples.

“But what happens is that our youth, when exposed to that, they either become [influenced] or become copycats,” Paraiso said. “That’s what we’re preventing here in the Philippines.”

NVE is a loose online subculture that glorifies violence not in pursuit of a traditional political or religious objective, but as an end in itself.

CICC: Video spread can cause further harm

The hearing also turned to the livestream of the Zamboanga shooting, which remained on Facebook for 14 minutes.

CICC said it gained visibility of the livestream about five minutes into the incident and reported it to Meta. Meta subsequently took the video down, but Hontiveros questioned why another 9 minutes passed before the livestream was removed.

Paraiso said the problem was partly jurisdictional: the CICC does not have jurisdiction over social media, gaming, messaging, or streaming platforms whose parent companies are based abroad.

He also said that while the CICC has trained itself and its partners to work with platforms’ community standards, the longer-term solution is for the Philippines to have greater jurisdiction over the platforms.

The concern is not merely the original violence. Hontiveros raised the contagion effect — the possibility that violent material can be repeatedly shared, glorified, and used to influence potential copycats.

Paraiso agreed that every second that such a video remains available can create harm, particularly when violence is rewarded with virality and sharing.

The CICC asked Meta to take down the videos and preserve the data for investigators.

Meta was not present at the hearing.

Hontiveros said the committee itself had found videos of the Zamboanga shooting still available on Meta’s platforms and pushed back against the idea that the CICC should be responsible for constantly finding and reporting them.

“Meta itself has to do better,” Hontiveros said. She said the company has enormous reach and responsibility over its platform and should not leave the CICC to clean up harmful content.

“Siguro hindi dapat CICC ang magligpit ng kalat ng Meta,” she said.

“Linisin niyo ang kalat niyo, ang basura niyo sa inyong powerful platform, linisin niyo. Huwag niyo iwan lahat sa CICC.” (It shouldn’t be the CICC that cleans up after Meta. Clean your mess up, your trash on your powerful platform. Don’t leave it up to the CICC.)

The CICC, for its part, continues to encourage the public to report videos and provide URLs so these can be relayed to Meta for takedown.

Hontiveros also questioned whether Meta’s artificial intelligence systems could detect an active shooting without waiting for a user or government agency to report it.

Paraiso said Meta’s detection systems are “hit or miss,” particularly for a livestreamed school shooting where there may be no specific text description or other parameter for the AI to detect.

But he also noted the difficulty of relying on AI to detect such instances. AI may not be immediately capable of understanding the context of a video in real time, especially if it doesn’t have a text description.

Paraiso said the CICC is still waiting for the release of a cyber warrant before it can fully investigate the digital devices and online activity connected to the case. He warned that even after a warrant is issued, obtaining information from platforms can take time because of jurisdictional issues involving companies based overseas.

“Based on experience, we ask for information. It takes about two months before the information gets back to us,” Paraiso said.

He said the CICC is working with the Supreme Court to hasten the issuance of cyber warrants, including addressing what he described as a need to strengthen the judiciary’s capacity to assess evidence involving cyber warrants.

Hontiveros appealed to the Supreme Court to recognize the urgency of the issue.

The problem, Paraiso said, extends beyond social media. Authorities can encounter jurisdictional limitations involving messaging, gaming, and streaming platforms, making it harder to obtain information or act quickly when harmful activity is detected.

He said the CICC wants stronger Philippine jurisdiction over such platforms.

There is also an operational gap in the ability of authorities to examine digital devices once they have them.

But lawyer Jewel dela Cruz of the Child Rescue Coalition pointed out that the government needs to examine whether law enforcement agencies have sufficient capacity and resources to conduct digital forensic examinations.

Paraiso acknowledged that the CICC has licenses for digital forensic tools but said their availability is regionally limited. Because school shootings and other NVE-related incidents can happen outside Metro Manila, he argued that these capabilities need to be expanded to provincial and municipal law enforcement units.

Along with addressing concerns on mental health, parental responsibilities, gun restrictions, and enhanced security protocols, Hontiveros stressed the importance of regulating digital spaces where NVE spreads.

“Seryoso po natin itutulak ang Child Online Safety and Protection Act. Sa panukalang ito, paparusahan ang pag-iimpluwensya sa mga bata na gumawa ng karahasan, tataasan ang responsibilidad ng mga internet intermediaries, at papalakasin ang kapasidad ng law enforcement para mabilis na magresponde sa mga banta… Ang isang lipunan kung saan kailangan bunuin ng bata ang takot na mabaril para lang pumasok sa school ay hindi isang lipunan na dapat nating taggapin,” Hontiveros said.

(Let’s push for the Child Online Safety and Protection Act seriously. With the proposal, we will punish those who influence children to commit violent acts, raise the responsibility of internet intermediaries, and strengthen law enforcement so they can respond faster to threats… A society where a child must deal with fears of being shot at school is not a society we can accept.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler Recap: How do recantations impact Ombudsman probe vs Romualdez?

The Office of the Ombudsman says it has 28 other witnesses ready to testify against Leyte congressman Martin Romualdez

World.title: How – and why – the Belo Medical Group defines ‘beauty’ as ‘longevity’
World.content:
Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Belo Medical Group and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

The beauty industry is fast-paced and ever-evolving, and everyone wants to be the pioneer of a new discovery or service – but a slow burn worked for Belo Medical Group, the Philippines’ pioneer in aesthetic medicine.

Case in point? The freshly opened Xiglo clinic, Belo’s first regenerative aesthetics and wellness clinic, is mainly focused on precision longevity.

Located on the 11th floor of 1 Proscenium at Rockwell, it is the latest reflection of Belo’s long-standing medical expertise and world-class care, spanning skin health and aging, focus and sleep, weight management, performance and recovery, women’s health, and men’s health.

“I’m sure you’re wondering, ‘Why did Belo only get into this now?’ Because there have been a lot of people who’ve been doing longevity for a few years,” Dr. Vicki Belo herself said during the launch event.

“The reason we did it only now is because we’ve been researching, we’ve been studying, and we really don’t do anything halfway. We want to make sure that everything is science-based,” she said, explaining how they’re the only clinic that has partnered with the experts in longevity – this includes the Asian Hospital and Prof. Dr. Dominik Thor, the president of the Geneva College of Longevity Science, who serves as Xiglo’s international medical advisor.

Backed by science and careful planning

“I know a lot of doctors, hundreds that we train; a lot of them are actually afraid of their patients nowadays because they come in with tons of ideas. They have peptide stacks put together by AI, they have their trackers, they have their Oura Rings, they have all that information,” Dr. Thor said about longevity, and the quest to make sense out of everything to create a meaningful journey. “I’m happy to say that Belo really has a mission of bringing that together in a responsible fashion[…]”

He added, “Longevity is integrative; there are so many components that are important: lifestyle, psychology, and obviously, there is a medical component to that, too. And we need great people that guide us.”
