World.title: Swill waters run deep
World.content:
“Apropos David Sayers’ soft drink saga (C8), in my teens, I worked at the local lolly water factory in Muswellbrook in the holidays,” writes Denis Cartledge of Tenterfield. “It was a Friday afternoon event for one particular worker to be thrown in the softwater tank that supplied the factory. He rarely washed, and his workmates thought they’d help his cleanliness regime. Looking back, I don’t think the tank was drained, cleaned and/or refilled. It was around that time we decided to stop buying a mixed crate of lolly water every few months.”

The current dress code discussion (C8) is revealing a few workarounds. Here’s Bev Matthews of Wallerawang: “Back in the early ’80s, three friends and I tried to get into a club in Parramatta. One of the boys had a collarless shirt on, and they wouldn’t let him in. I happened to be wearing a knitted cardigan with a collar (like I said, it was the ’80s). He donned it, and voilà, they let him in.”

“In the late 1970s, my brother-in-law went for an after work beer at the Manly Yacht Club in Brisbane, of which he was a member,” says Colleen Riga of Potts Point. “Clad in his work gear consisting of boots, stubbies and polo shirt, he was told that club rules required a tie for evening entry. They had no problem with the work gear, so, looking through a box under the counter containing ‘emergency neckwear’ they presented him with a clip-on bow-tie (or ‘blowfly’ as he incorrectly heard) and he was free to enjoy a coldie.”

Reading about Mash McDonald’s in Iran (C8) reminded Ann MacKenzie of St Ives of the time she was in Tehran in 2017 and noticed a fast food establishment dubbed ZFC.

In reply to Stephen Tait’s inquiry into the wellbeing of Dirranbandi pubsters the Norton Brothers (C8), Janice Creenaune of Austinmer says the visit was earlier in the year, on Anzac Day in fact, and that the pub was “heaving with 2-up patrons. However, today we are off to camp near the ‘Hog and Billy’ in Girilambone, (known colloquially as ‘Girl’ I believe). Is there anybody we can look up for you there, Stephen?”

World.title: When will accountability and international law mean something?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters When will accountability and international law mean something? August 20, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. When will accountability mean something? The Israeli military’s decision to close its investigation into the killing of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and six colleagues, without criminal charges, should disturb every Australian who believes that international law applies equally to all (″⁣Wong outraged as Israel clears soldiers″⁣, 20/8). Australia’s own independent review commissioned by the federal government and led by former Australian Defence Force chief Mark Binskin found a “significant breakdown in situational awareness” and serious failures to follow IDF procedures. Yet, more than two years later, the soldiers responsible face no criminal prosecution. In effect, Israel has investigated itself and declared that there is no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct.

This is not merely about one tragic mistake. It is about what happens when institutions responsible for accountability are allowed to define their own failures as insufficient to warrant accountability. The same pattern of euphemism and institutional self-protection is evident in the wider catastrophe in Gaza. We should not allow words such as “mistake”, “failure” or “complex conflict” to obscure the human reality of thousands of civilian deaths.

Silence is not neutrality. Nor is demanding accountability by Israel’s government and IDF. When will we all feel free to speak out as humanitarians without being targeted as antisemitic?

Chris Trueman, Southbank Israel is no friend of Australia’s

Australians have every right to feel outraged by the whitewash of the killing of Zomi Frankcom, along with several of her colleagues, by Israel’s IDF. As Penny Wong noted she learnt of Israel’s decision on World Humanitarian Day moments before it was announced – a fact that was “especially insulting to Zomi’s loved ones, humanitarians and all Australians”. The constant refrain from the Israeli IDF, ″⁣nothing to see here″⁣, is not surprising when one considers the overwhelming numbers of so many innocent lives, aid workers, medicos, journalists, civilians killed in Gaza with little or no accountability. It is not the first time the Israeli ambassador has been called to account for unacceptable treatment of Australians given the humiliating and appalling treatment of those Australians attempting to deliver aid to Gaza as part of a flotilla. When are we going to wake up. This morally bankrupt Israeli government has shown it is no friend of ours. Stern measures must be imposed. Sending the Israeli ambassador packing and imposing sanctions must be considered and not before time.

Anne Moorhouse, Inverloch More than a slap on the wrist needed

Every Australian should be outraged by the Israeli Defence Force’s decision not to pursue a criminal investigation into the killing of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom in 2024. This deserves much more than a slap on the diplomatic wrist by Penny Wong.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris



Send the ambassador home

The response by the Israeli Defence Force investigation into the death of Zomi Frankcom and her six colleagues defies comprehension. With hundreds of bullet holes found in the car, just what does the IDF think was going on? It is about time the State of Israel be sanctioned, and the ambassador sent home.

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn Outrage is a good start, now action

Penny Wong is outraged that Zomi Frankcom’s killers were cleared of criminal conduct. Well that’s a good start. Outrage by itself achieves nothing though, it is what comes next that matters. And what did come next? The Israeli ambassador was called in for a rebuke. A rebuke that will also achieve nothing. Outrage needs to be channelled into decisive action. Australia must step up.

Lorel Thomas, Blackburn South THE FORUM A service faltering

The 4 Corners program on the parlous state of the aged care system was concerning but no surprise. The current government and minister are not wholly responsible. It’s been all downhill since My Aged Care was introduced in 2015. An out-of-touch bureaucracy and workers bogged down in endless, tedious reports have clogged the system.

The insensitive and inefficient algorithm introduced last year is just the final insult.

I worked for an Aged Care Assessment Service for 15 years, and the daily grind of filling out the pitiless documents was a constant source of frustration. When I started working in hospitals

35 years ago, the ACAS forms were two pages long; when I finished last year, they could come to 76 pages. More thorough reports have not enabled any older person to get improved or quicker services. Quite the opposite.

4 Corners highlighted the issue whereby the system, including the algorithm, was seemingly designed by public servants and not tech experts with expertise in complex system design and was also not trialled satisfactorily before being introduced.

Terry Kelly, Coburg Right priorities

I have heard the government is rolling out cuts to the NDIS. I have also heard of the idea of a 25 per cent gas tax on companies that are making extraordinary profits.

Here’s an idea: Let’s have the gas tax and use that money for the NDIS.

Bill Proctor, Launching Place



Change and risks

We can only hope that as the state election draws nearer, those toying with the idea of voting for One Nation will give serious attention to where their vote actually goes. With a lack of serious policies, and some questionable candidates (″⁣Zero policies and a blank page: Is Pauline Hanson serious about Victoria?″⁣, 20/08), One Nation poses a real threat to governance in Victoria. It is easy to tell a pollster that you want change for its own sake. It takes much more effort to seriously consider what that change would actually mean.

Be careful what you wish for.

Judy Williams, Beaumaris Labor still a chance

Resolve Political Monitor polling shows primary support for Labor has fallen two points to 25 per cent since the elevation of Ben Carroll to the top job (″⁣New leader fails to lift Labor’s poll slump″⁣, 19/8). However, primary support for the Coalition is only at 27 per cent,

7.4 points below what it achieved at the 2022 election. The indicative preference flows from Labor and One Nation voters to the Coalition might give it a 53-47 lead over Labor, but clearly on primary numbers, Labor is not without a chance of securing a fourth term.

Other positives for Labor are the 17 per cent drop in support for Jess Wilson as preferred premier from last month’s RPM survey and the 43 per cent of respondents undecided on their preferred premier. Labor should be encouraged by these numbers. Voters will be aware Liberals have had a cavalcade of leaders (Wilson the ninth since Jeff Kennett) and have shown themselves wholly unfit for government. Labor needs to keep reminding voters that a vote for the Liberals is a vote for infighting and dysfunction.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne Food security needed

While Europe bakes and burns, and penguins struggle to keep a footing (“Fears for future over shrinking sea ice”, 20/8), we’re reminded daily that change is here. In the face of change, China yet again reminds us of the importance of agency over key fundamentals – our energy, housing and food (“China’s breakneck plan to safeguard its food future”, 20/8).

China views “food security on par with defence as an existential imperative for national survival”. The push to energy and food dominance as China’s Politburo seek to “reach 70 per cent or more of the world food (and energy) market in less than 15 years” serves to remind us of our own food and energy sovereignty.

With recent experience of the perils of relying on others’ oil, the time is nigh for us to fast-track our plans for energy and food independence and export. With half of our energy now coming from wind and solar, we’re powering up, but what’s our 15-year food security plan?

Karen Campbell, Geelong Heeding unpaid work

I would like to see the Australian census asking more detailed questions about unpaid community work. The current form features only a single yes-or-no question about whether a person volunteered for an organisation in the past 12 months. It does not measure the actual hours spent, unlike the detailed weekly data collected for paid employment.

Unpaid work makes up an enormous part of our economy and contributes to our productivity.

The contribution by older people, the unemployed, young people, and others who cannot work or are on the margins of society is not adequately acknowledged. This information would also assist in the development of policies that support volunteers and community-based organisations, and include them in our mainstream economy, particularly relating to environmental outcomes and social services.

We should not be replacing paid work with free labour.

Volunteering often allows us to recognise and develop our full potential when paid work does not tick these boxes.

Jennie Epstein, Little River Regulating gambling

The regulation of gambling is not just someone else’s problem. We all need to ensure that politicians take proper responsibility for control of an industry that has such potential to harm vulnerable members of the community.

In spite of the recommendations of the Murphy report, it seems the government is not listening and has got things badly wrong.

As other letters correspondents have noted, opting out is not an option. There is no need to advertise gambling; the only people who benefit are the vested interests who are never satisfied.

The industry should be required to acknowledge its harmful effects and invest in rehabilitation programs. Public opinion is clearly sending a message that must be heard.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor



Preschool lessons

In response to columnist Sally Rawsthorne (“Has play got in the way of learning?“, 18/8), as a parent, grandparent and paediatric occupational therapist, the preschool years are about learning through play-storytelling, measuring, making everyday objects work, sharing in the playground and classroom.

Children do the formal learning at school but need the motor skills to control a pencil, use their imagination to tell a story with words, objects or in drawing, sit on the floor, open their lunch box, and get to the toilet independently.

Forget the photograph of Sammy the Sloth and printing it off – draw it together.

Less technology leads to more joy in parenting. And keep the lunch box contents simple.

Debbie Isaac, Hawthorn East Different forums

Your correspondent (Letters, 19/8) highlights the modern scourge of anger and outrage everywhere on social media, and writes that he thinks it’s worse than gambling s.

Recently, I dipped my toe into this murky world of commentary on politicians and made a few negative comments on YouTube clips that were overwhelmingly pro-One Nation and hostile to the federal Labor government.

What struck me was the vehemence and aggression in the commentary. The plethora of conspiracy theories and homophobia was startling.

I couldn’t wait to extract myself from the netherworld of hate and bile. I think I’ll stick with the pleasant and civilised Age letter-writing community.

David Fry, Windsor Driving south

Good to hear that Sydneysiders aren’t rev-heads like us Victorians, Chris Harrison (Comment, 19/8). Down south, if you venture into the right lane to overtake someone while doing the speed limit, you’re likely to be tailgated. And good luck getting back out of the right lane – you’ll have to dodge between a phalanx of tradies’ utes weaving and zooming past.

Susan Yell, Warragul Taxing encounter

I recently rang the Australian Tax Office and was apprised via a recorded message that it was introducing voice recognition technology to replace identification procedures.

I’m not convinced that, given the combined sophistication of deep fakes and AI, this is a step in the right direction or that the ATO is as technologically competent as it thinks it is.

I was even less convinced after ATO staff successfully disconnected my call twice and then struggled to manage the ″⁣on hold″⁣ function leading to several three-way conversations with a confused help desk and ″⁣escalation″⁣ manager.

Fortunately, unlike my right to gamble, voice activation is opt in. I think the ATO is taking a gamble on this. Stephen Farrelly, Donvale Fear of banning

Your correspondent (Letters, 20/8) highlights the success of Australia’s ban on smoking advertising. That is exactly what the gambling industry is afraid of.

Peter McGill, Lancefield



The Wright stuff

I have read Tony Wright’s columns for longer than I can remember. The Age should publish a collection of his articles over his extensive career. It would become a journalists’ handbook for wit and grace. May he enjoy retirement from daily duties, watching gannets plunge, brolgas dancing and riding his motorbike through western Victoria.

But please don’t stop writing.

Luke Mills, Richmond Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Gambling

Who in the Canberra political class believes that a problem gambler has the necessary willpower to take the opt-out option in the new gaming laws? The ads are part of the addiction.

Peter Roche, Carlton



After the watered-down gambling bill I opt-out of voting for Labor, the Coalition and One Nation.

Greg Malcher, Hepburn Re gambling reform, as Bill Shorten would say, “The Big End of Town” has won. Pity all the little blokes.

Warren Thomas, Ivanhoe Furthermore

Israel’s finding of no wrongdoing into the death of Zomi Frankcom should come as no surprise (″⁣Wong outraged as Israel clears soldiers″⁣, 20/8). What possibly could that country have done wrong?

Julian Druce, Balaclava A standard line of my upbringing was – parent to child – ″⁣We don’t want to hear what you want″⁣. Voters are saying the same thing to what are fast becoming the two major political parties of Australia’s past.

Ruth Farr, Blackburn South You don’t even need to be a Rhodes scholar to see potholes are a big issue for drivers in Victoria.

Robin Jensen, Castlemaine



It’s time Australia had a distinctive national flag. A competition should be held for people to suggest designs and then a panel to select six and then those six to be voted on in a referendum.

John Walsh, Watsonia Best way to end a drought in the UK? Schedule a Test.

Bryan Fraser, St Kilda West Donald Trump’s overture to North Korea overlooks the assistance, in both military personnel and weaponry, provided by Kim Jong Un to Putin’s war on Ukraine.

Garry Meller, Bentleigh Finally

Thank you Tony Wright for your humour, warmth, decency and clear-sighted analysis. We’d love more of your entertaining columns, if only now and then.

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick

World.title: Turnbull-backed battery proposal sets off sparks in Doreen
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCity life Turnbull-backed battery proposal sets off sparks in Doreen Adam Carey August 20, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A renewable energy company chaired by former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull plans to build a large-scale battery on bushfire-prone land in Melbourne’s green wedges, alarming nearby residents who lived through the devastating Black Saturday fires of 2009. The proposed lithium-ion battery energy storage system could potentially store enough electricity to power almost 90,000 homes for a day. It would be built at an estimated cost of $500 million. Locals Sarah Hunter, Alicia Hynes, Barbara Marshall, Gareth Davies and Mel Nelson stand opposite the proposed big battery site. Ruby Alexander But the project has startled the small semi-rural communities of Doreen and Arthurs Creek on Melbourne’s north-eastern fringe, where residents only learnt of the proposal when a handful of neighbours were contacted by a communications agency on Tuesday. The Middle Hut BESS project, which had been kept under wraps until this week, is at an advanced stage of planning, with its developers, Turnbull Renewables, poised to apply directly to the state government for a planning permit next month.



Turnbull Renewables said the property had been chosen because it sat beneath two high-voltage transmission lines, meaning the battery could be plugged directly into Melbourne’s energy grid. “The site sits along the existing 330kV and 220 kV high-voltage transmission lines, the backbone of Victoria’s electricity network … [It] has been strategically chosen to store and dispatch energy close to metropolitan Melbourne,” the company said. It said the site was one of few along the transmission line corridor with the environmental conditions needed to support a battery system, and had been positioned away from homes. The battery system would cover about 14 hectares of what is currently mostly paddocks. But the site is also in a green wedge area that is zoned for its environmental significance and is designated as bushfire prone. A creek running through the property has Aboriginal cultural heritage value. The terrain is hilly and accessible only by a narrow gravel road.



Sarah Hunter lives on Middle Hut Road, where she and her husband run a small egg farm more than a kilometre away from the proposed battery site. She was not informed of the project on Tuesday; she learned about it through a local chat group. Hunter said the battery system would industrialise the mostly agricultural area, characterised by its rolling hills and native wildlife, and used as a foraging area for the critically endangered swift parrot. “There is a place for batteries but not in the middle of a hilly area in the green wedge with a bushfire overlay,” she said. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips What happens when your EV runs low on a regional road trip? I found out Ben Groundwater Travel writer “It’s like a transformation of this beautiful area in the foothills of the Kinglake mountains. When you put in a big industrial site, that’s really damaging.”



Arthurs Creek resident Gareth Davies lives a few kilometres away, on a property at the foot of Mount Sugarloaf that came under direct attack on Black Saturday. “I just don’t think it’s the right place,” he said. “Everybody would say that, like it’s a NIMBY thing, but my concern is it’s a known bushfire-prone area. I could barely get insurance. I had to ring around like you wouldn’t believe to get insurance here because of the risk that the actuaries put on this area.” Middle Hut BESS is the first Victorian project for Turnbull Renewables, a company chaired by Malcolm Turnbull and founded by his wife, Lucy Turnbull. It has previously delivered two hydropower projects in NSW. Malcolm Turnbull told The Age the battery system would store excess wind and solar power generated during the day and dispatch it at night. “Storage is absolutely critical for the energy transition,” he said. “With more and more of our energy coming from wind and solar, and particularly solar storage, the ability to essentially time-shift electrons from the middle of a sunny day to the evening, is really vital.”



Former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull says the Middle Hut BESS will assist the energy transition. Dominic Lorrimer The former Coalition prime minister, who left politics in 2018, said the developers had reached out to the local community, and would host a public information session later this month. “We are confident that this is a good project. It’ll be good for all of us,” he said. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last The project is expected to be considered by Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny under the significant economic development provisions of the planning scheme.



A Victorian government spokesperson said the Department of Transport and Planning had not received an application for the project, and that all proposals were considered on their merits. “Green wedges play an important role in supporting agriculture, jobs, tourism and open space around Melbourne, which is why we are strengthening protections for them,” the spokesperson said. A Nillumbik Council spokesperson said they were aware of the proposal but it would not be assessed by council. “We believe the proposal will need to be publicly advertised, giving residents and other interested parties an opportunity to make a submission or object,” they said. According to Turnbull Renewables’ project timeline, construction would begin in 2028 and the battery would be operational by 2029.



A fire damaged Neoen Energy’s Victorian big battery project in July 2021. The fire burned for three days. Channel 7 Middle Hut BESS would be one of the largest lithium batteries in Melbourne, with a proposed capacity of 290MW/1160MWh. A small handful of industrial-scale batteries have already been built around Melbourne’s fringes, including the Melbourne Renewable Energy Hub in Plumpton, Rangebank BESS in Cranbourne West and the Victorian Big Battery near Geelong. Victorian election Zero policies and a blank page: Pauline Hanson doesn’t look serious about Victoria Chip Le Grand State political editor The Victorian Big Battery caught fire and burned for three days in 2021. Turnbull Renewables acknowledged Middle Hut BESS was proposed for a bushfire-prone area and said a fire-risk assessment would form part of its application. It said it was engaging with the CFA. World.title: Police commissioner apologises for miscommunication after family told that deceased bushwalker was alive
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWTragedy Police commissioner apologises for miscommunication after family told that deceased bushwalker was alive Riley Walter and Jack Gramenz Updated August 20, 2026 — 7:49pm ,first published 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW Police will investigate a series of failures that resulted in officers mistakenly informing the family of missing bushwalker Lily Hooper that the 18-year-old had been found alive after an eight-day search in the state’s Southern Highlands. Commissioner Mal Lanyon on Thursday was forced to apologise for the miscommunication that devastated her grieving parents, who, moments earlier, had celebrated what they believed was a miraculous survival. Loading Missing hiker Lily Hooper was found dead after an eight-day search in the NSW Southern Highlands. NSW Police For almost 20 minutes on Thursday, Hooper’s family believed she had been found alive in dense bushland before being told police were still working to determine her condition. Shortly after, police confirmed she had been found dead.



“I don’t know exactly what was said to her parents at the time, but obviously her condition, when she was located, the initial information that had been reported and was communicated, was that she was alive,” Lanyon said. NSW Police Commissioner said he apologised “unreservedly” for the miscommunication. KATE GERAGHTY A police officer at the search base, on the edge of the Nattai National Park, told Hooper’s parents, Jim and Kirrily Hooper, that the teenager was alive after an SES volunteer found her during a ground search. An elated Jim Hooper told reporters that he had never given up hope that his daughter would be found alive. On the eighth day of searching, he had laid a “charm” – his daughter’s guitar and a pack of Tim Tams – under the marquee the family had turned into a makeshift home since August 12. It was to beckon their daughter out of the bush. “She’s coming home,” he said through tears before loved ones celebrated at the search base.



“I’ve been beside myself ... we found her.” The miscommunication may have been sparked by a radio code believed to be used by SES searchers to report that a body has been found, in which they refer to full, half or empty water bottles to signal whether a person is alive in the event family members may be monitoring the radio. A half bottle of water is believed to indicate a person’s condition is unclear. Hooper’s mother said police had told her she was found alive with half a bottle of water in her possession. Police do not use the code during their own searches. Australian Army personnel who participated in the rescue operation are addressed on Thursday. Kate Geraghty “That miscommunication, I unashamedly apologise for any additional trauma that may have caused Lily’s family, but certainly for the embarrassment and confusion that caused,” Lanyon said, adding that police sought to correct the information at the earliest opportunity.



“The miscommunication, obviously, was born out of elation that Lily had been found and her condition at that time was such that searchers were relieved and certainly those at the command base were elated.” NSW SES Assistant Commissioner Colin Malone said information transmitted over radio communications could be broken up in remote areas. Lanyon on Thursday afternoon apologised to NSW Premier Chris Minns, who had earlier announced to a parliamentary budget estimates committee that Hooper was alive after he received the incorrect information. SES volunteers involved in the search for Lily Hooper. Kate Geraghty “I’ve got some terrible news, and I apologise to the committee. But it seems as if the early advice was wrong, and Lily’s body’s been found, and she’s been found deceased,” Minns said.



The information was passed from police to the premier via Police Minister Yasmin Catley, which Lanyon said was not unusual for a high-profile investigation. “The communication may have passed through a number of hands,” he said. “We will obviously look at that communication, how it took place, with a view to making sure we confirm that.” Lily Hooper began her hike on the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail on August 12. Kate Geraghty Lanyon had spoken to NSW SES Commissioner Mike Wassing and would review the failure, he said.



“This is not a circumstance I would like to see repeated,” Lanyon said. “What’s important now is we look at the communication between all agencies to make sure we improve it.” Almost 1000 searchers had scoured dense bush in the national park looking for Hooper since she was reported missing on August 12, having left her home in Sydney’s south-west that morning to hike the Bonnum Pic walking trail. The beginning of the trail. Kate Geraghty Police officers on horseback, motorcycles and from several units searched alongside Australian Defence Force personnel, NSW State Emergency Services volunteers and Rural Fire Service firefighters.



Helicopters and thermal imaging technology had also been used during the search for the teenager, who had remained in contact with her family on the day she went missing. Police found her Hyundai parked at the bottom of the challenging Bonnum Pic trail shortly after her family reported her missing. Emergency services gathering at the search site on Thursday. KATE GERAGHTY Authorities on Thursday evening were working to retrieve Hooper’s body from dense bush that Lanyon said could not be accessed via police helicopter. Her cause of death is yet to be determined and will be subject to a coronial investigation. Specialist officers were exploring the possibility of carrying Hooper’s body out of the bush, given the difficulty to access the site where she was found, which was not on a clear walking track, and was a significant distance from her car. It is unclear what injuries, if any, she sustained or when she died. The rescue operation combed through the Nattai National Park, south-west of Sydney. NSW State Emergency Service



“We’ll now work through a process, whether it’s manually, whether it’s on foot, to retrieve her body,” Lanyon said. “We’d like to bring her back to be with her family.” NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane, who had earlier, citing media reports, posted on social media that the teenager had been found alive, said Hooper’s death was heartbreaking and an unimaginable loss. “So many people had been hoping for Lily’s safe return and today’s news will be difficult and deeply felt,” she said. Australian Army soldiers involved in the search on Thursday morning. KATE GERAGHTY



Federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, Hooper’s local member, published and then deleted a social media post indicating she had been found alive, later saying the incorrect reports of her survival made the family’s loss even worse. “We can only imagine what Lily’s family is going through right now. Such news would be a nightmare for any parent, and we grieve for Lily’s wider family,” Taylor told parliament. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the family’s loss was an unspeakable tragedy. “Lily Hooper had so much more to offer the world. Her passing, I have no doubt, will be felt very deeply,” he told parliament. “Our thoughts are of course with her family and loved ones on what is an incredibly sad and difficult day.”



MPs also rose for a moment’s silence. Wollondilly Shire Mayor Matt Gould said the council’s performing arts centre and library would be lit up in purple for the rest of the week in Hooper’s memory. Flags on the council chambers will be flown at half-mast. “They are small gestures, but I hope they help show in some way just how deeply Lily’s loss is being felt across our community, and how much Wollondilly is thinking of her family, friends and everyone who loved her,” Gould said. World.title: Sevens superstar named for Wallaroos debut as Ballymore becomes golden headquarters
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Sevens superstar named for Wallaroos debut as Ballymore becomes golden headquarters Iain Payten August 20, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sevens superstar Maddison Levi is set to make her 15-a-side debut for the Wallaroos against New Zealand on Saturday, but her sister and Aussie sevens teammate, Teagan, who has been outstanding for the Titans during an NRLW stint, will not be released to play for the Jillaroos at the Rugby League World Cup. The developments came as Rugby Australia chairman Daniel Herbert hailed a $40 million redevelopment of Ballymore that will make the iconic Brisbane venue the new permanent home of the Wallaroos and national sevens programs. Loading Herbert said the goal was to complete the Wallaroos’ move to full-time status by the end of the year after RA, the Queensland Rugby Union and the Queensland government unveiled plans to turn the eastern stand at Ballymore into a “Teams in Gold” high-performance headquarters. Along with state-of-the-art facilities, there will be a new training field built on the eastern side. Construction will start later this year and is hoped to be finished before the 2029 Women’s Rugby World Cup in Australia.



The new facility will complete a rebirth of Ballymore, which is owned by the QRU and once staged Test matches and Reds games, before falling into disrepair and being deemed unsafe. The western stand was rebuilt as part of a $31 million project in 2022. The facility will effectively be the first home for Australian women’s rugby, and also house the men’s sevens program and the Wallabies when they are in Brisbane. The two sevens programs are based at RA headquarters in Moore Park, but have to rotate training fields in eastern Sydney. “We want our teams to be world-class, and we’ve always wanted to give them a world-class base,” Herbert said. “Ballymore gives us the opportunity to do that. It’s going to be one of the best rugby facilities, not just in the country, but anywhere that I’ve been and seen. So, it’s hugely significant and very exciting. “Having those teams out there training together, training around the Reds – men’s and women’s – and having the community able to come and watch, it’s fantastic.”



The construction of a new headquarters is the latest in a string of developments in the Australian women’s game and follows the appointment of Tim Walsh as the new director of women’s high performance, Reg Tayler as his successor as national sevens coach and Sione Fukofuka as the new Wallaroos coach. Maddi Levi runs away to score yet another try. Getty Images Fukofuka’s appointment last week, and the search that preceded it, drew criticism for being far too drawn out, given Jo Yapp departed as Wallaroos coach in September. Fukofuka will not take over the side until 2027, as part of a release agreement with his previous employers, the Scottish Rugby Union, so Walsh is serving as interim coach along with Mike Ruthven, Ben Mowen and Tayler. Loading



Walsh, who coached the women’s sevens team to Olympic gold in 2016, told the Inside Line podcast this week the next big task was moving the Wallaroos into a full-time program by the end of the year. “We’d like to do that this year,” Herbert said. “We’ve started to see that with the placements we’ve made with Tim Walsh and now Sione. We’ve got a team over there with a pretty experienced coaching team around him for the Wallaroos Test match this week. You can see the integration there that Tim’s already started. ” The Wallaroos will play their 100th Test on Saturday when they take on New Zealand in Auckland, and though Australia have never beaten the Black Ferns in 30 attempts, the addition of sevens superstar Levi could help them make even more history. Levi is one of Australia’s most dominant sevens players, having scored 270 career tries since making her debut in 2021. She trails Kiwi Michaela Blyde by only 17 tries on the list of most World Series tries.



Levi has been named on the bench for a probable debut in the second half. Evidence of Walsh’s plan to share more sevens and 15s talent between the formats is also seen in the Wallaroos backline, which also contains halfback Tia Hinds, centre Alysia Lefau-Fakaosilea and winger Maya Stewart, and Bienne Terita and Levi coming off the bench. Walsh told Inside Line he hoped to also have Teagan Levi as an option for the Wallaroos in the future, after the Aussie sevens star returns from a stint in the NRLW. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Wake-up call for us’: Waratahs brace for change after Cheika return is confirmed Teagan Levi has been in red-hot form for the Titans, prompting questions about whether she could extend her short stay in league and be available for the Jillaroos at the Rugby League World Cup in October and November.



But Levi’s contract with RA stipulates she must return to rugby after the NRLW season on October 4. “I’d love to see Teagan with an Olympic gold medal around her neck [in 2028] and then play at a home World Cup [in 2029],” Walsh said. “Post-NRLW season, she will be back training, preparing for round one of the World Series [in Dubai on November 28-29]. She will be returning after her commitments with the Titans.”

World.title: A photo op or nuclear talks? What Trump wants from a meeting with North Korea’s dictator
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaNorth Korea diplomacy A photo op or nuclear talks? What Trump wants from a meeting with North Korea’s dictator Lisa Visentin August 20, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: Not for the first time in his second term, Donald Trump has dangled the prospect of a revived face-to-face with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un. The US president repeatedly returned to this theme throughout 2025, at one point telling reporters he hoped talks would eventuate by the end of the year, always invoking his apparent good chemistry and rapport with Kim. There is no public record that the two men have directly communicated since they last met more than seven years ago, when Trump crossed into the North Korean Demilitarised Zone in June 2019. The high-optics summitry later collapsed without a breakthrough to roll back Pyongyang’s nuclear program. Donald Trump last meet face-to-face with Kim Jong-un when he crossed into North Korean territory in 2019. AP And so Trump’s off-the-cuff assertion,“Yeah, I will be”, when asked by reporters on Wednesday (US time) if he expected to meet Kim this year, will be met with some scepticism.



He added that North Korea had “57 very powerful nuclear weapons ... If I were president, I wouldn’t have allowed it, but he’s got them”. Related Article Updated

Trump diplomacy Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul Experts have noted it is an oddly specific figure. While it broadly aligns with estimates dating back to 2017, some analysts believe Kim’s stockpiles to be much higher, pointing to his turbocharged nuclear program in the years since the talks with Trump. This week, Trump matched his bravado with a tangible overture to Kim, scaling back joint military drills with South Korea while sideswiping Seoul as a mendicant ally and talking up Pyongyang as “unthreatening and respectful” on his watch. “The pullback was the first concrete move by the president to engage North Korean leader Kim Jong-un this term,” seasoned Korea expert Victor Cha noted in an opinion piece in The Washington Post.



It follows the same playbook Trump deployed after his Singapore summit with Kim in 2018, when he suspended military drills with South Korea. It has fuelled speculation that Trump wants to meet Kim during a trip to Asia for the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, and is looking for a foreign policy win that can distract from his self-made quagmire in Iran. So far, the Kim regime’s response can be generously described as coy. The North Korean leader’s influential sister, Kim Yo-jong, said the curtailed military exercises changed nothing, and Pyongyang test-fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles on Thursday afternoon, a day before the drills are due to end. Yo-jong denied there was any direct communication between Trump and Kim, but described their relationship as “still excellent” and said her brother had fond memories of the US president. Loading Ultimately, the more consequential factor in this saga is not whether the men will meet, but what they will talk about if they do. The stakes change dramatically depending on whether Trump is searching for a photo op, similar to his meeting last year with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Alaska, or wants to restart a dialogue with Kim on nuclear weapons, says Peter K. Lee, a research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul.



“There is a growing sentiment both in American policy circles and elsewhere that this [denuclearisation of North Korea] is no longer a viable option, if it ever was,” Lee says. “That remains a lodestar for South Korean policy. There can be no recognition of North Korea as a nuclear state.” Russian President Vladimir Putin joined China’s Xi Jinping and Kim Jong-un at a Beijing parade marking the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II in September. KCNA via KNS via AP Experts have long argued that officially abandoning denuclearisation could open a Pandora’s box in East Asia, fundamentally weakening confidence in the American deterrence commitments and forcing South Korea and Japan to reconsider their no-nuclear defence positions. Trump has already tacitly acknowledged North Korea as a nuclear power, potentially recalibrating the benchmark for any revived talks in favour of Pyongyang, which is desperate to be recognised as a nuclear state.



Meanwhile, North Korea is not the same diminished, hermit state it was a decade ago, when the focus of bilateral talks was on denuclearisation. New revenue streams are flushing through its economy courtesy of its bolstered alliance and weapons supply to Putin’s Russia. It has also entered the war in Ukraine, and has improved trade and relations with China. Related Article Analysis

Trump diplomacy Pivot from Asia? What Trump’s South Korea ‘shock’ says about US strategy “The only thing I can possibly see that Kim would be interested in is if somehow it was almost known at the outset that North Korea would get some type of de facto recognition of its nuclear status,” says Mason Richey, a professor at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul. The week has left South Korean President Lee Jae Myung juggling tricky dynamics while his trade emissaries were in Dallas trying to broker a way forward on a stalled $US350 billion ($490 billion) deal with the Trump administration. He’s been forced to suck up a public blasting by Trump, who gave him no forewarning of his order to cut short the military drills the evening before they began.



At the same time, Lee hails from the progressive left in South Korea that wants engagement with Pyongyang, and has previously urged Trump to play a “peacemaker” role while identifying his own role as “pacemaker” in supporting those efforts. In a late-night tweet on Wednesday, Lee commended Trump for scaling back the military drills and his “efforts to create conditions for dialogue aimed at establishing a peace regime on the Korean Peninsula”. Trump scaled back joint military drills with South Korea the evening before they began this week. AP And yet, Trump’s unilateralism, wild unpredictability and fondness for dictators will also ramp up anxieties that any dialogue between him and Kim will cut Seoul out of the process altogether. The South Koreans have a term for it: Korea passing.



Which raises another question: What might China’s role be in all this? In a stroke of coincidental timing, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi was in Seoul this week, his first visit in five years, as the two countries forge warmer ties – part of Beijing’s diplomatic push into the crevices created by US uncertainty. “The US should change its longstanding hostile policy towards North Korea,” Wang said when asked whether Beijing would mediate a summit between Trump and Kim, distancing China from the process. China quietly stopped calling for North Korea’s denuclearisation in 2023. Would it really be content with sitting on the sidelines for major talks concerning Pyongyang’s weapons capability, its only official ally?



The swirling dynamics make for an interesting summit season when it kicks off in the coming weeks. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: No excuse for toxic off-field behaviour, but there is an explanation
World.content:
August 20, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two decades ago, I sat in my office at Sydney University and watched an incredibly fit young man in his late 20s break down in heaving sobs. He was an elite footballer at the top of his game playing with one of the leading NRL clubs. He’d asked to meet. He said he wanted to get something off his chest. At the time, I was a pro bono gender adviser to the National Rugby League and was working with a team of researchers to understand the off-field culture of the game following an alleged group sexual assault in Coffs Harbour. Illustration by Matt Golding When the then CEO of the NRL, David Gallop, approached me in 2004 about conducting education with the players, I told him that there was no point running programs that were not grounded in real-world scenarios. So we surveyed all the players about off-field behaviour and we followed up with in-depth interviews. We repeated the research every five years and designed and evaluated education programs based on what we learnt. What surprised me most was the honesty of the players. Many of them wanted to talk. In the case of the man sobbing in my office, he wanted to clear his conscience. He told me about staying in a hotel on an away game and becoming aware that a group of his teammates had taken an extremely inebriated young woman back to a hotel room.



He said he wanted to intervene but hesitated because one of the guys was a star player. The next morning, he saw the young woman stumbling down the hallway in tears. “That’s stayed with me,” he said. “Her expression. I knew something really bad had happened. The look on her face will stay with me forever.” Related Article Updated

AFL off-field behaviour Drugs involved in hotel room incident with Swans players and two mystery men The Sydney Swans are currently facing their own reckoning over off-field culture with five players stood down for breaching the club’s standards. There are also allegations that a sexual assault occurred. No-one has been charged. It’s heartening to see that much of the media commentary, including by the AFL, has focused on the importance of supporting any woman who might have been harmed. And that’s a big shift from the days when women who partied with footy players were dismissed as “groupies” and the only thing that mattered was what happened on the field. We’ve come a long way since I started working with the NRL. I clearly remember an arrogant corporate type laughing at me for suggesting there should be an elite women’s league. He thought “breasts” were not designed for body contact sport. Seriously?



What we are still not discussing is what we know about making lasting change in the male-dominated world of elite football. Without ever excusing gendered violence or harassment, it is critical to see that young men playing elite sport are thrust into a culture of extremes. On one hand, they are disciplined to within an inch of their lives when it comes to training, diet and performance. On the other, they are expected to adapt overnight to making money their everyday peers can only dream of, to fame, to the desire to “cut loose” after a big win and to lots of people who want to party with them. Related Article Opinion

AFL off-field behaviour I played for the Sydney Swans. Time will tell what the club truly values Brandon Jack Commentator and author How they adapt varies with the level of support they get from senior players and their clubs. Education programs have to be grounded in real-world scenarios that they encounter off the field in their surreal lives. I’ve long held that we owe it to these young men to give them a chance to talk openly about real-world situations they face off the field with educators they can relate to. At the NRL, we used ex-players working alongside professional educators.



Education that works is sustained, engaged and delivered by people who are motivated to make lasting change around the horrific rates of gendered violence. Dannielle Miller, director of education at Women’s Community Shelters, is a good example. Her programs focus on understanding young men rather than simply lecturing them. Former Swans player Brandon Jack has written a compelling novel, Pissants, about the brutal and misogynistic culture that sometimes defines off-field bonding in the AFL. But it is equally a book that examines male loneliness and uncertainty in the face of an enormous pressure to fit in with the group. In Helen Garner’s latest book, The Season, she follows her much-loved grandson’s under-16s footy team. A passionate AFL supporter, she sees “a kind of poetry” in the grit and grace of team spirit. Garner’s book is characteristically generous, reflective and insightful. It’s a book that asks a critical question: what is it like to be poised on the brink of manhood today? As for the five key Swans players stood down for breaching their club’s code of conduct, the club and the AFL should be commended for acting swiftly and putting the broader culture of the game ahead of what happens on the field. Catharine Lumby is a professor of media at the University of Sydney. She was a pro bono gender adviser to the National Rugby League for 15 years. World.title: Big names back for All Blacks as team to play Springboks revealed
World.content:
The All Blacks have recalled several star players with Cam Roigard, Will Jordan and Damian McKenzie named to start in this weekend's test against the Springboks in Johannesburg.

The trio return from injury to take their place in the side while Ardie Savea resumes the captaincy duties after being rested for the first three games of the South African tour.

Savea is at No.8 with coach Dave Rennie retaining the loose forward trio from last month's win against Ireland, with Luke Jacobson at openside and Tupou Vaa'i at blindside.

Ardie Savea scores a try against Ireland. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

Codie Taylor is at hooker with Tyrel Lomax and Ethan de Groot the starting props.

There was plenty of speculation as to who would play lock and Rennie has gone with Fabian Holland and Josh Lord in the second row, with Vaa'i to provide cover.

In the backs, Roigard returns at halfback with Ruben Love at first-five and Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea in the midfield.

McKenzie has overcome the ankle injury that ruled him out of the win over the Bulls last weekend and will start at fullback, with Jordan and Josh Moorby on the wings.

Rennie has gone with a 5-3 split of forwards and backs on the bench, which includes front rowers Asafo Aumua, George Bower and Fletcher Newell, loose forwards Peter Lakai and Anton Segner, midfielder Anton Lienert-Brown, halfback Kyle Preston and outside back Leroy Carter.

Damian McKenzie celebrates a try with teammates. Photosport

Rennie said they can't wait to run out on Ellis Park on Sunday morning (NZT).

"After all the build up and anticipation, our whole touring squad is excited to get this first Test underway," Rennie said.

"We have selected a balanced mix of big match, experienced players and younger players who have earned the right to play in this first Test."

Rennie said the three games against the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls in South Africa have proved invaluable as they prepare for their biggest challenge of the year so far.

"The first three franchise games have exposed our newer players to the way South African teams play and have been fantastic in helping us build combinations and develop the game we want to play.

"We know the Test series will be a huge step up. We're well aware of what the Springboks will bring to the contest and the pressure that will come to bear. They are number one in the world, playing at their spiritual home in front of their passionate fans, so we will have to be at our very best on Saturday."

Josh Moorby in action against the Bulls. Photosport

Savea, Roigard and Jordan will make their first appearance of the tour in the match, while Savea and Taylor are playing their 110th Tests.

It will be Savea's 18th Test against South Africa and Taylor's 17th.

Segner and Moorby will be playing the Springboks for the first time.

World.title: Wellington residents march on Parliament in bid to get rising water bills lowered
World.content:
Hundreds gather in Wellington to protest new Tiaki Wai bills Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Some Wellington residents are fed up and stressed by the prospect of rising water bills as they marched on Parliament in a bid to get the organisation to lower costs.

And a former Wellington mayor-turned MP, who turned out to the protest, admitted his was among councils which could have invested more in water infrastructure in previous years.

About 300 people turned up in central Wellington on Thursday to raise concerns about their water bills in a cost of living crisis, as part of the Stop Tiaki Wai group.

Water bills are increasing by 13.3 percent on average across the region this year, and are projected to reach over $6000 per year in a decade.

A sign at Thursday's protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Lower Hutt resident AJ said that's shocking.

"The people are fed up, you can't get blood out of a stone can you?"

She said her first water bill was about $500 for the quarter.

"I came out here today, because the cost of living is through the roof, and this is just one more bill that people have to find money to pay - and people can't find that money anymore."

Mary Head, an Upper Hutt resident and pensioner, said she's frustrated about the way her water bills were being calculated.

"There's only my husband and I at home, and the amount of water we use, is negligible to say a family - and yet we are paying the same or more of a family of six or eight," she said.

Mary Head at the protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Tiaki Wai said in its first years' of operation, the way water services would be calculated was taken from councils' rates bills.

In Upper Hutt, Porirua and Lower Hutt water bills were being calculated through a combination of a fixed rate and property value.

In Wellington city, most people's bills were based on property valuation, board chairperson Will Peet recently told RNZ.

The entity has said it wants to move to a single-pricing model in the future, as well as install water meters.

But Head said the indicative costs Tiaki Wai had put out for that so far - at half-a billion dollars for the programme - were ridiculous.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns admitted he couldn't actually stop Tiaki Wai - which was set up under the government's Local Water Done Well policy.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Nunns said he would be paying his bill this year - but suggested he would encourage people to not pay their bills if the costs didn't change.

That's not something Wellington City Councillor Karl Tiefenbacher, who was among the crowd at parliament, agreed with.

"I don't think that really works. To be fair I am against the fact we have no rates cap on top of Tiaki Wai - I think that's the issue."

He asked what the point of rates caps against councils were, if there was none against water entities.

"I think water is the biggest issue we have. I think this protest actually represents what is wrong with our society at the moment, and that's that it's becoming unaffordable."

When asked whether he thought spending was needed to upgrade failing pipes and water plants, Nunns said "no one" was happy with the current state of infrastructure.

Attendees at the protest on Thursday. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"We have always paid for water infrastructure in our rates, people have not necessarily understood that, they'll be understanding it now - but at $2200 a year, and until recently I was the sole occupant of the property, that's not realistic."

New Zealand First MP and former Wellington city councillor and mayor Andy Foster was also at the protest.

He was asked whether the council he led between 2019 and 2022 did enough to invest in pipes during its years in power.

He said his council set in motion more investment and was heading in the direction of a CCO for infrastructure, but also said more could have been done.

"We were going to fix it, so long term, yes, there was under-investment in infrastructure, but that is true of pretty-well every council in the country."

Tiaki Wai said it needed to spend $25 billion dollars across three decades to fix the regions old failing water treatment plants and pipes.

Stop Tiaki Wai protest attendee, Bridie McGill with her sign. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Officials said there's a major crisis point at Seaview, where a crucial outfall pipe was leaking into the harbour and the Waiwhetū stream.

They also said about 100 kilometres of pipe at the point needed to be replaced each year.

In a recent interview with RNZ, Tiaki Wai chief executive Michael Brewster urged anyone facing hardship to contact the organisation, saying Tiaki Wai had policies in place to help those who were really struggling to pay bills.

But he said debt collection would have to be pursued for those who were refusing to pay for no reason.

"If you are refusing to pay the bill and not contacting us then we, we would unfortunately, we would have to pursue that.

"Because at the end of the day there is an obligation to pay the bill, if nobody pays their bill we've got no money to fix the system."

Attendees march to Parliament. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said on Thursday, he respected the rights of Wellingtonians to join the protest and express their views.

But he urged the protesters to respect those working at Tiaki Wai trying to upgrade the region's infrastructure.

World.title: Former Tauranga mayor says he wasn't warned about landslide risk amid damning review
World.content:
A former mayor of Tauranga says warnings about the landslide risk on Mount Maunganui never reached him in his 12 years at the helm.

A damning review by former High Court judge Paul Davison KC found the council failed to act on several warnings over the course of 27 years about the risk of a slip on the nearby campground.

Stuart Crosby was mayor of Tauranga for 12 of those years, from 2004 to 2016.

"I watched online as Mr Davison gave his report, and to say it was confronting is an understatement," he said.

"Very disappointing in terms of the failure of processes within Tauranga City Council to get the right information to the right people to make the right decisions."

He said he hadn't been told about the slip risk.

"The areas that reached us were two, one was with regard to rockfall which we ... addressed, and the second was to put in fire prevention," he explained.

"Certainly to the best of my knowledge I don't remember receiving any information about mitigating landslips."

Former mayor says landslide risk warnings never reached him Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

He said it was a wake-up call for other councils.

"In fact, this morning I wrote an email to my own council, I'm on the Bay of Plenty Regional Council, requesting a report to go to our council with regard to information flow, and I'm sure this is happening up and down New Zealand," he said.

As for whether councils should look back through their records for any warnings they had missed, "I'm pretty sure they're doing it as we speak, I'm quite confident of that."

Dr Tom Robinson, a senior lecturer in disaster risk at the University of Canterbury, said the failings of Tauranga City Council weren't necessarily exclusive to it.

"What the report clearly shows is there are systematic errors, not just in Tauranga Council, that's the one that's been exposed here but those systematic problems that it's identified exist across the country," he said.

He echoed the sentiment that councils across New Zealand should consider the report a wake-up call.

"This is an opportunity for councils and organisations around the country to re-evaluate, look at some of the hazards and risks they're responsible for, and think about what actions they need to take," Robinson said.

"I think the problem, though, comes back to: councils have a huge amount of tasks and huge amounts of responsibilities, and dwindling reserves to be able to do that."

He said not enough money was spent on prevention.

"We've known for decades that a dollar spent on reduction reduces the amount you spend on response and recovery by 5, 7 or 10 dollars, you get the money back, and yet we're still putting the ambulance at the bottom of the hill and responding afterwards," he said.

World.title: Ombudsman shines light on 'coercive and unlawful treatment' at Wakari Hospital
World.content:
A Wakari Hospital patient with intellectual disabilities was almost constantly locked in their bedroom for at least 18 months in conditions the Chief Ombudsman says amounted to prolonged solitary confinement.

Inspectors for the Ombudsman visited the inpatient unit for adults with intellectual disabilities in Dunedin in March.

Last month, Chief Ombudsman John Allen shared the findings, saying inspectors observed some of the worst practices they had witnessed and some treatment amounted to torture.

Health New Zealand confirmed plans to close the ward on the same day, while the Ministry of Health said it would launch an independent investigation that would consider if allegations of human rights abuses should be referred to the police.

John Allen released a longer summary of the concerns and urgent recommendations on Thursday, detailing observations under the heading "punitive, coercive and unlawful treatment".

Inspectors detailed a model of care that appeared to prioritise containing and restricting patients to minimise the immediate risk of physical harm, with little attention given to providing meaningful rehabilitation or person-centred care, the report said.

The ward has faced significant criticism before, with a previous ombudsman calling it "a disgrace".

Dunedin's Wakari hospital inspected under crimes of torture Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

But the March inspection was triggered by an innocuous visit to check on a refurbishment Health New Zealand said would be underway from mid-2025, which would require patients to be relocated.

During an unannounced visit in October 2025, Ombudsman staff members discovered the refurbishment remained largely in the planning phase and patients had not been moved out.

They became "very concerned" about patients seen living in restrictive environments, flagging this with ward management and government agencies before sending an information request to Health New Zealand.

In December 2025, Health New Zealand confirmed a high level of restrictions remained at Ward 10A.

It prompted that four-day announced visit in March.

"We became very concerned about the conditions and treatment experienced by tāngata whaikaha (whaikaha means 'to have strength, to have ability, otherly abled, enabled')," the report said.

"We were concerned that the practices of the ward were extreme, fostered institutionalisation, risked traumatising tāngata whaikaha and may have constituted abuse."

Inspectors observed that one patient was locked in their bedroom "almost unceasingly" with extremely limited contact.

"We were very concerned that the physical arrangements were increasing the institutionalisation of this tāngata whaikaha, which had persisted for at least 18 months," the report said.

"We considered these arrangements may amount to prolonged solitary confinement."

The attempts to expose the patient to the ward also appeared to be very limited.

"At the time of the inspection, their bedroom door was being unlocked and left open for 90 seconds each day (rather than 30 seconds previously)," the report said.

The Ombudsman said it expected coercion was not used to modify behaviour and tāngata whaikaha had choice where possible.

Instead, the report outlined a pattern of staff incentivising good behaviour so patients could have their basics needs met including losing access to the toilet while in seclusion, being told they would only be able to see a dentist if their behaviour stabilised, or not being allowed to buy things with their own money unless they complied with staff directions.

"We were highly concerned about the potential use of punitive, coercive and unlawful practice on the ward."

Chief Ombudsman John Allen Supplied

Inspectors found patients might not have consented to some of the medication and sedatives they were given, including intramuscular injections.

This is not legal except in limited circumstances.

A bariatric EVAC mat was used to restrain and move patients, resulting in friction burns for some patients, despite the Ombudsman saying the United Nations' Special Rapporteur on Torture had raised concerns about the use of similar restraints and how they should only be used for legitimate medical reasons.

"In our view, moving a tangata whaikaha to a seclusion room is not a 'legitimate medical reason' envisaged by the Special Rapporteur," the report said.

Helensburgh Cottage, which was meant to help people to transition to care providers in the community, had remained empty since the pandemic despite the Ombudsman noting it appeared to be a better environment to provide care.

Staff told inspectors that it was not being used due to staffing pressures.

While detailing facts about Ward 10A, the Ombudsman noted that previous inspection reports found the physical environment was not fit for purpose - a description the former District Health Board also used.

The Ombudsman's concerns were detailed to senior staff at Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health after the visit, before urgent recommendations were made.

Allen did note that the relevant agencies had taken swift action in response to the concerns and recommendations.

The Ombudsman's recommendations included:

Health New Zealand urgently improving the "conditions of detention" by ending all prolonged isolation and improving physical living arrangements, activity and care.

Ending the use of bariatric EVAC mat to restrain and move tāngata whaikaha.

Urgently take measures to ensure the individual safety and rehabilitation of all tāngata whaikaha on Ward 10A.

The Ministry of Health making sure an independent investigation was undertaken.

Immediately reviewing the medications prescribed to tāngata whaikaha on Ward 10A, to ensure that all medication is lawfully prescribed and administered.

Immediately implementing a model of care in Ward 10A that focusses on tāngata whaikaha well-being and rehabilitation.

Health New Zealand previously said it was taking the allegations made by the Chief Ombudsman and others very seriously.

"We take patient safety and care very seriously and want to acknowledge the patients, their families, and our staff, all of whom we are supporting during this period of change," a spokesperson said.

"Our focus remains on ensuring the safety, dignity, and rights of the current patients, while strengthening oversight and reviewing practices."

Health New Zealand planned to undertake a wider review of forensic intellectual disability services nationally, and said it had already enhanced clinical oversight, reviewed patient care and rehabilitation plans, strengthened approaches to reducing seclusion, and strengthened governance arrangements.

World.title: National MP Greg Fleming breaks ranks, criticises Budget tax change
World.content:
A first-term National MP has criticised a tax change the government has introduced, saying a plan to cap the donation tax credit has "zero" logic.

Maungakiekie MP Greg Fleming said work was underway to "fix" the cap, but the minister responsible said that was not the case.

Fleming was speaking at a charity sector political hui in Wellington on Thursday, when he was asked about the logic behind the $100,000 donation cap limit.

"Zero," he responded. "I've no problems with being quoted publicly on saying I think it was an error."

At the Budget, the government made changes to the charity tax credit rules, which would mean no more tax credits once donors give more than $100,000 to charities.

Individuals could claim a third of their charitable donations back as a tax credit, as long as the value of their donations did not exceed a third of their annual total taxable income.

The $100,000 cap will affect about 350 donors when it is introduced next April, but they represent about 10 percent of donations claimed or about $103 million.

In a regulatory impact statement, the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) said the government spent about $350 million a year on tax credits.

IRD took the view that there was no conclusive evidence the credits actually lead to more giving, and that there was a risk of bad actors and misuse, such as those claiming the credit in advance of the funds being applied to charitable purposes or deriving a private benefit from the donations.

When the cap was announced in May, Revenue Minister Simon Watts said it would ensure the donation tax-credit scheme remained financially sustainable and would also limit tax-planning risks that arose when a donor made a gift to a charity they controlled themselves.

The charities sector has expressed concern that the cap may make would-be donors consider dialling back their donations at a time the sector was already struggling - a view Fleming appeared to agree with.

Fleming said he understood why the cap had been brought in, but there were a "myriad" ways to fix the misuse of donor-advised funds, without introducing a cap.

He said the cap was a "sledgehammer to crack a walnut" and further changes would be made.

"I'm advocating really, really hard for this and I can assure you that work is underway to to fix that," he said.

Watts said Fleming's comments were not correct and the government's position had not changed since the Budget.

"These changes resulted from IRD concerns that, in some cases, the tax credit was being misused for tax planning purposes," he said. "The change does not come into effect until 1 April 2027 and only affects donations over $100,000.

World.title: Nursing graduate applies for more than 100 jobs without success
World.content:
Nursing graduates who have applied for hundreds of jobs and have not found work say it's devastating to hear there's a shortage of nurses.

The nurse's union says Aotearoa's health system is falling into a deeper crisis, with emergency departments and wards bursting at the seams.

It follows revelations that Health New Zealand has hired just 54 full-time equivalent nurses in the past two years.

Nursing graduates struggle to find work while hospitals in crisis Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The situation is driving some graduates to consider making the move to Australia... joining their course mates who have already left.

After finishing hundreds of unpaid placement hours in Auckland, Megan completed her Bachelor of Nursing late last year.

In Aotearoa, new nurses have to apply for graduate positions, some do this through Te Whatu Ora's application system called ACE.

Others apply directly to private hospitals, community organisations and primary care.

But since graduating in March, Megan has applied for more than 100 nursing jobs and hasn't had any luck.

"I feel like I've failed, or there's something that I'm not showing in my application. I didn't realise it was going to be this hard to get a job."

Megan told Checkpoint she's getting by on the Jobseeker benefit while she continues to look for work.

If she can't find work soon, she's eyeing up Australia and said she may be forced to give up on nursing entirely.

"If I don't get a job I'm either likely going to have to re-study something else, or go into a completely different workforce.

"The running joke at the moment is that I become a flight attendant, which I don't really want to, but I've got to get a job somewhere."

Megan said it doesn't make sense how hard it is to find work because of reported shortages and staff burnout.

"We see constantly that the hospitals are understaffed and people are dying.

"Going into an election year, how can you promise us as nurses, new grads and even the public that the hospitals are going to be staffed?"

Hearing stories of graduates not being able to get work has students worried too.

Eden Sandhu is in her final year of studying nursing at Ara Institute of Canterbury.

But seeing nurses the year above missing out on jobs has made her anxious.

"Like thinking that there's no guarantee of securing a graduate position is just draining.

"We're told that there's a shortage, but all of us still experience anxiety that people aren't getting jobs, will there be a position for me when I graduate?"

To get their degrees, nurses have to complete hundreds of hours of on-the-job training, which is not paid.

Eden Sandhu said she had sacrificed so much financially to become qualified and worried about the future.

"[It's] a huge a worry because I've got a family and a mortgage... it's not okay to have graduates coming through having to consider after three years, to find something else."

Moving to Australia is something that's been on Eden's mind over the past few months.

"I think if New Zealand focused on supporting the students through placement, offering paid placements, upping the amount nurses are paid for the incredible stress levels they carry.

"Focussing on how to keep nurses here and not have such a terrible environment that people need to shoot off, that would change how I feel about leaving," she said.

"I would want to stay, I do want to stay, but unfortunately [if I don't find a job] I can't."

Dawn Blyth, the Nurses Organisation's National Student Unit co-leader, is also in her final year of study.

People in her cohort have already applied to Australia's graduate programmes.

"I graduate in November... we understand that jobs aren't guaranteed anywhere in any climate.

"But what is really hard to understand is how can we be saying that our country is so short of nurses... when there isn't the funds to put those nurses into jobs."

Health New Zealand national chief nurse Nadine Gray told Checkpoint they were offering a similar number of roles to last year to keep a mix of experienced and graduate nurses.

She said they were supporting all graduate registered nurses into employment, but this might not happen immediately, and they had never been able to employ every graduate nurse.

World.title: Former Alliance candidate Mary O’Neill sentenced for harassment of Napier neighbours
World.content:
A former local government and parliamentary candidate has been warned she could end up in prison if she does not stop harassing her neighbours.

Mary Jelena O'Neill, 62, was sentenced in the Napier District Court on Thursday for a single charge of intentional damage.

The offending happened in Napier, but O'Neill appeared via an audio-visual link from Dunedin, where she now lives.

The charge, which was proven against her at a judge-alone trial this year, was laid after O'Neill hired a contractor to cut back trees on the property of her neighbours on Napier's Bluff Hill.

However, Judge Russell Collins said the heart of the matter was not the physical damage caused but a "cynical act of harassment" towards the neighbours.

O'Neill has a previous history of harassing the same neighbours - including four breaches of a protection order in 2021 - and other people, dating back to a charge of threatening behaviour in 2015.

Court documents from 2021 say she made "false and damaging" accusations of sexual misconduct about one of her neighbours to the authorities and on social media.

She also once threw a rock at an AA serviceman who had been called out to fix a neighbour's car, then drove towards him, stopping about 60cm away.

Judge Collins stopped short of imposing a custodial sentence on O'Neill, saying she had "complex needs" and her claims about the neighbouring family were "delusional".

Instead, he imposed a maximum term of two years of intensive supervision by a probation officer.

The supervision includes conditions that O'Neill lives at the Dunedin address and does not go near her former house or neighbour's house on Napier Hill.

She will also need to do any counselling thought necessary.

She is not allowed to contact her victims or post anything about them on social media.

Judge Collins warned O'Neill that if she breached her intensive supervision, or reoffended, "I doubt that you would avoid a term of imprisonment", or at least an electronically monitored sentence such as home detention.

O'Neill stood unsuccessfully as a candidate in the Hawke's Bay Regional Council elections in 2019 under the name Jelena Jordan.

She was previously an Alliance Party candidate for Parliament in 2011 and 2014.

This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Woman and child seriously assaulted during Northland break in, man arrested
World.content:
A woman and her child were injured in an assaulted during an alleged break in at a Northland property.

Police have arrested a 38-year-old man following what they called a "violent aggravated robbery" in Kaikohe at 7am on Thursday.

Detective Senior Sergeant Aaron Crawford said police were called to a report of a man allegedly carrying a gun, breaking into a property on Williams St.

A woman and her child were inside, Crawford said, and the pair were "seriously assaulted" before a man fled in a car he stole from the home.

The police Eagle helicopter found the car a short time later in Ōmāpere.

Crawford said the man police believed was involved attempted to run and allegedly tried to steal another car by assaulting another person.

Police intervened, Crawford said, and took him into custody.

A gun and items police believed belonged to the home of the woman and child had since been found, he said.

The woman was taken to hospital in a serious but stable condition, Crawford said, and the child had minor injuries.

"Both are understandably shaken," he said.

The 38-year-old man was in custody and Crawford said charges were pending.

Police wanted to hear from anyone who saw what happened on Williams St or any sightings of a yellow Suzuki Swift travelling west on SH12 towards Whirinaki, Kouto Loop Rd and then Opononi and Ōmāpere.

They also wanted to hear from anyone who saw a man acting "suspiciously" in the Ōmāpere area on Thursday morning.

Information could be provided online at 105.police.govt.nz, or by calling 105 and using the reference number 260820/5258.

World.title: Swans sponsors pull support in wake of allegations
World.content:
A number of brands associated with the Sydney Swans have suspended their activities with the club in the wake of a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault in Melbourne on Monday.
